Esteban Martínez, Comte de la Expedición' — a 2nd reference to the 1788 Expedición del Norte (NW-coast/Russia-precursor; cf. n272). Orig. p.206.

summary: 'Padrón de ganados' (SF livestock census) — on the Asesor's dictamen that settlers keep '15 vientres y un padrón (padre) de cada especie de ganado,' may freely slaughter/sell the surplus; non-pobladores may slaughter/sell freely without keeping breeding-stock. (Same run: Argüello→Fages 2 Jul, duplicate revista/fuerza extracts.) Orig. pp.75, 221.

author: José Argüello
themes: indian-raiding; indigenous-warfare; neophytes; santa-clara; serranos; amador; women; 1788
summary: 'Sobre pelea de Indios' — the gentiles of the ranchería next to Mission Santa Clara fought the 'Serranos,' with several *Cristianos* (neophytes) of the mission taking part; Sgt. Pedro Amador dispatched, found 2–3 Christians already flogged by the friars (RR. Ministros); he reprimanded the *cabecillas* of all the neighboring rancherías, warning that if they again 'convidaban algunos cristianos para sus alborotos, serían castigados,' and punished the Christians likewise. ⭐⭐ Second incident: a Gentile called 'el Corporal Trabajador del Pueblo' (a mission-Indian work-foreman) 'andaba haciendo una junta para ir á dar guerra á otros Gentiles por una muger' — seized, given 'unos azotes,' freed after 3 days' arrest. Indigenous inter-group warfare + a woman as *casus belli* + neophyte participation + a mission office-holder leading a raid (cf. Doc 139). Orig. pp.225–226.
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, p. 225–226, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 4, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 261–262 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n261–n262)

author: Pablo Cota; Goycoechea

summary: Purísima construction (Cota, 24 Ago): the mission *cuadro* 'cerrado' + a rebellín, houses done by mid-Sept, 5 families arrived + 2 more coming — 'La Misión ya tiene 79 cristianos.' ⭐⭐ Goycoechea (1 Oct) reports the return of Esteban Martínez from 'la Expedición del Norte' on the fragata *Princesa* (the 1788 Martínez–Haro Alaska voyage — the one that found the Russians, precursor to the 1789 Nootka crisis); + a fragata anchored at SF on the 13th under Jph de Guiriarza[?] w/ the presidio *memorias*, mission *sínodos* & 8 servants. ✎ the volume's one NW-coast datapoint (Russia-driver/Bodega-precursor; no Nootka-*crisis* material — that = C-A 5). Pablo Cota dispatched (in 4–5 days) with the escort & servants 'á fin de hacer principio de estacada y habitaciones.' author: Goycoechea

Ortega replaces alférez Pablo Cota, by inventory. (@n295 top: a Savage note that p.332 of the originals reads '30 Setre 88 — Como lo solicita.') Orig. pp.333, 335.

Points read so far: (1–6) the two pueblos — fomenting San José & Los Ángeles with retired soldiers, the 1784 grain-purchase order, the suertes/solares/ejidos land distribution (San José de Guadalupe relocated off a barranca for fire risk), escoltas kept past the 2-yr limit, Vicente Feliz commissioned at LA from its founding, the annual alcalde/regidor elections under comisionado oversight (orders 1785–86); (7) ⭐⭐ the old missions' demographic decline from the 'Gálico' (syphilis) vs the flourishing new ones; (8) ⭐⭐⭐ neophyte flight + the troop expeditions to recover them ('por la mala dirección de los Curas'), and Fages's preferred method — trusted Indians + gifts to the ranchería captains rather than force; (9–10) ⭐⭐ refusing the friars' escort demands (approved 13 Jan 1790 Nº886) + humane-march instructions; (11) the archive indices; (12) Neve's price-tariffs (aranceles), adjustable by abundance/scarcity; (13) ⭐ the excessive Real-Hacienda cattle → annual *matanza* (cf. the Apache/horse warning, Doc 139); (14) horse/mule breeding off the Sonora line at presidios/pueblos/missions; (15) refusing the missions' attempts to buy military goods from the troops; (16) ⭐ the prohibition on trading with the Manila galleon (Nao de Filipinas) at Cabo San Lucas (+ Bucareli's ban on friars boarding it); (17) the San Blas–California trade duty-free 5 yrs (from 11 Oct 1786); (18) ⭐ this 'comercio pasivo' harmful — the only cash entering is the limited situado for troop pay (cash-scarcity). ⏳ Continues past n159 (points 19–20+ on the *cambalache*/foreign-ship commerce control, per the earlier gap-sample at ~n160).

themes: mission-critique; indian-cruelty; neophytes; diet; confinement; punishment; labor; sitjar; antonio-de-la-concepcion; peyri; san-miguel; church-internal
summary: THE FRIAR-WHISTLEBLOWER DOSSIER ON MISSION-INDIAN TREATMENT. Fr. Antonio de la Concepción (Fernandino, sent 1797 to found Mission San Miguel) charges the P. Presidente Fr. Buenaventura Sitjar with being 'totalmente opuesto á cuanto está mandado por R. Cédulas… en orden á la crianza y educación de los indios': a dispute over teaching doctrine in the natives' own language (Sitjar) vs. Castilian (the cédulas); improper same-day adult baptisms; letting baptized Indians flee to the hills. Sitjar had him declared 'loco,' violently removed from the mission, and beaten on the road to Monterey (witnesses Fr. Antonio Peyri, Fr. Juan Manuel Fernández, Fr. Diego García, the presidio surgeon, & pilot Esteban Martínez). ⭐ Attached interrogatorio on mission conditions (numbered answers): neophyte housing (adobe/tile for married; single women & single men locked in dormitories at night by the padres); labor hours (winter 3+3, summer ~4, exempting pregnant/nursing/old/children); diet — *atole* morning, *pozole* midday & evening, 'que en el año no alcanza á 22 fanegas de grano por individuo' (deemed insufficient); clothing (a cotton blanket + 1–2 *frazadas*); punishment (the padres rarely consent, but the *gente de razón* & escort guards punish them, esp. at Mission San Francisco); language (missionaries 'indifferent' to Castilian); no Christian Indian to the hills 'sin licencia limitada'; the missions' cash/credits (San Carlos 862 p, Soledad 221, San Antonio 536+410, San Luis Obispo — 4 partidas = 1,966 p). A rare *insider* (friar) indictment of California mission discipline & material conditions — the 'Indian-cruelty charges' the completion plan flagged (the 15-question interrogatorio, answered by a first respondent, runs n60–n70)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XVII, p. 90–…, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 10, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 49–69+ (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n49–n69)

author: Felipe de Goycoechea (SB commandant)
themes: mission-critique; indian-labor; coercion; diet; confinement; goycoechea; temporalidades; church-vs-state
summary: ✓ VERIFIED vs scans n71–n72 (2026-07-07): the diet answer verbatim — 'por comida dos cucharadas de pozole é trigo cocido… á la tarde por cena otra tanto atole; carne le da por semana para uno ó dos días… por insuficiente, para que con sólo esto se mantengan y puedan RECIBIR las fatigas á que se les obliga' ✎ *(the manuscript reads 'recibir,' not 'resistir')* — and the causal link explicit: this is 'la próxima causa de que muchos… se van pasando á robarla de la Misión, ó á las fugas.' GOYCOECHEA'S ANSWERS to the 15-question interrogatorio — a secular official corroborating the mission-cruelty charges 'con la verdad que solo bajo mi palabra de honor': doctrine taught in the native language then Castilian (1ª); ⭐ the ordinary diet — morning *atole*, midday *pozole* + wheat, evening *atole* w/ meat 1–2×/week — 'insuficiente para que con sólo esto se mantengan y puedan recibir las fatigas á que se les obliga' (the food question); ⭐ single women & single men locked in a room/*pozolera* within the Mission at night, released by the padres each morning (only Sta Bárbara has a recreation room; 8ª); labor hours/tasks, pregnant & nursing exempt (9ª); ⭐⭐⭐ 12ª — the missions PREVENT & PUNISH Indians who occupy themselves with soldiers (*gente de razón*), so the Indian is barred from earning wages & the food/clothing improvement he'd gain — 'por esto se retarda visiblemente la civilidad de estos indios'; the missionaries peg their sales to the *arancel* yet recompense poorly (13ª); the *temporalidades* run with hidden 'máximas' (14ª); + an attached table of the missions' debits with the SB habilitación (San Gabriel 3,311 p, San Juan Cap. 1,627, Sta Bárbara 1,696, Purísima 405, San Buenaventura 1,611, San Fernando 267…; n80). A presidio commandant testifying, on his honor, that the mission labor system coerces & impoverishes the neophytes — with Doc 52 a two-witness indictment.
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XVII, p. 105–…, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 10, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 71–80 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n71–n80)

Rodríguez will put to the American sailors [left by the *Eliza*] 'y con particularidad al que entienda algún otro idioma': (1) how many English ships they've seen on the NW Coast ('la altura'), their ports, forces, captains' names & destinations; (2) at what points they conduct their *peletería* (fur) trade & how they trade with the Indians; (3) whether the English are settled ('de asiento') at Nootka or the Columbia… The full ~13-question set also probes the SANDWICH ISLANDS (Hawaii): foreign (English/American/Spanish) establishments there, European crops & livestock introduced, whether the native Hawaiian government has been subordinated to the foreigners, whether the English hold a fort/force there; and specifically the deserter *Francisco de Paula Marín* (the Spaniard who became Kamehameha's advisor) — with orders to cross-check the sailors' answers 'para sacar en limpio lo cierto.' PUNISHMENT: stocks, shackles, dark rooms, calabozos exist; 'the common punishment is azotes y grillos'; 'in my estimation the Padres lack more indulgence than rigor.' MISSION FINANCES: libranzas for 18 Alta Cal. missions total 12–18,000 pesos/year. DEFENSE OF SYSTEM: punishment 'has its origin in the very conquest of Antigua California, practiced for more than 100 years'; 'varying it could have fatal consequences.' PRESIDENTIAL AUTHORITY: witnessed 5 consecutive President appointments in Baja Cal.; missionaries shown cuaderno of 10–16 pages of spiritual faculties. author: Raymundo Carrillo
summary: ★★ INSTRUCCIÓN FOR FOUNDING OF MISSION SANTA INÉS — 18 ARTICLES. Complete military regulations for escort commander at new mission founding. Art. 1: troops serve as if facing hostile Indians. Art. 2: build enramada for guard post, store arms/munitions/provisions. Art. 3: day/night sentinel at commanding point. Art. 4: daytime cavalry custody, caballada corralled at night. Art. 5: soldiers never leave guard post. Art. 6: gentiles never enter compound armed; leave weapons at rancherías. Art. 7: treatment of Indians must be gentle ('suave'); no extortion; return stolen goods. Art. 8: trade (cambalache) only before escort commander; never provide arms, belduques, swords. Art. 9: soldiers never go alone to rancherías; punish violations instantly. Art. 10: rare punishment of gentiles; arms only against Christian Indians for theft or arson; moderate punishments. Art. 11: troops exist to propagate Gospel; must cooperate in construction (church, habitations, almacén, guard post, family houses); never send soldiers alone. Art. 12: treat missionaries with veneration; assist in attracting Indians. Art. 13: graduate escorts for Padres visiting rancherías proportional to Indian temperament and distance. Art. 14: do NOT dispatch parties hunting cimarrones (runaways) — troop too small. Art. 15: observe general orders from old missions. Art. 16: on day of toma de posesión and first Mass, write certification and send to Governor. Art. 17: coordinate provisions and arms with Carrillo. Art. 18: faithful compliance brings glory to God and career advancement. pp. 1053–56
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XVIII, p. 397–403, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 11, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 400–06 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n401–407)

Economy as the means: gold placers & silver mines on 'el Río,' whale fishery on both coasts, redwood (*Palo Colorado*) for shipyards, weaving-masters & a *maestro de primeras letras* per presidio; each province to get its own export buque separate from the San Blas Dept ships; warns *against* peopling with convicts, favoring families + orphans aged 10–12. 'Movimientos de Anglo-Americanos y peligro que amenazan'; advises shifting the Department of San Blas → Puerto de San Quintín; population increase = 'la primera necesidad de aquella colonia.' Complete: ends n29 with the Viceroy's decree ('Como pide el Sr Fiscal de Rl Hac.a'), authenticated copy by Conde del Valle de Orizaba, 20 Dec 1805. See expanded Entry C17 (verbatim quotes).

The foundational Russian-incursion intelligence report: on 14 Feb two Anglo-Americans presented themselves among the christian Indians from the other side of the port, saying they deserted a Russian frigate anchored at Bodega — one of the four men the 'Genl ruso D.n Nicolás Resanow' had held as exiled prisoners on the island facing the presidio (1806); three armed Russians appeared at the padres' house at 12¼. Coast clear from Punta de Bonetes to Punta de Reyes at writing; an Unalaska Indian sent [to Monterey] per the Gov.'s order. Published: Mathes (1990) Doc 3.

A foreign nation, apparently Russian, has established at the puerto de la Bodega — a fortification with artillery and ~100 individuals, mostly Russians from the establishments at Onalaska & Kodiak, agents of the Russian [American] Company, with the aim of opening commerce with the provinces; cites the treaty of alliance signed at Veliky Luki, 8(20) July 1812. Establishing in Spanish territory (the northern coast up to the entrance of Juca [Juan de Fuca]) violates the territory & treaties. Orders relayed to the Comandantes Generales of Nueva Galicia & the Provincias Internas (Baja Cal & Sonora) and the Comandante of San Blas.

author: Argüello
summary: 'Expedición militar — Combate con los indios': 22 Oct, 10 SF-presidio soldiers (mission launch) joined Sgt. Francisco Soto (from Mission San José; 2 soldiers + 100 Indian auxiliaries) to recover San José-mission cimarrones; night river navigation; reached a large, wooded, swampy island ranchería at dawn the 27th. Forewarned, the cimarrones had massed 4 rancherías (~1,000 armed Indians), posted sentinels, sent away women/children, and put up 'porfiada resistencia,' attacking from all sides. ~3-hour fight, driven off 'á vivo fuego'; the swamp (water knee-deep) let them swim to another Tulares island & escape — none captured but 'bien escarmentados.' The Indians had taunted that 'soldiers are worth nothing on foot, only on horseback,' then learned otherwise. Spanish loss: one auxiliary, 'Julio,' killed + one lightly wounded; heavy enemy loss. Soto praises the auxiliaries' obedience & valor. [→ military-history register.]

summary: Conde del Venadito → Gov. Has urgently ordered the Cmdt. Gen. of Provincias Internas de Occidente to send from Sonora a ship (the 'San Carlos' or another) with troops & munitions to San Antonio / Concepción, and alerted the Cmdt. Gen. of Nueva Galicia; expects Solá to dislodge the *facciosos* with the reinforcements + his troops + armed *paisanage*

summary: Conde del Venadito → Solá — the COLONEL-PROMOTION letter (= expanded Document 3 below; its page cite is corrected here from i.192–197). Acknowledges Solá's reports nº 174 (4 Nov) & nº 177 (12 Dec 1818) warning of two insurgent frigates preparing in the Sandwich Islands [Hawaii] to invade, and the attack on Monterey presidio after 18 Nov; approves the defense; thanks all in the King's name; confers on Solá the grade of *Coronel de Milicias Provinciales* (provisional despacho enclosed, published in extraordinary gazette). Recounts ordering the 'San Carlos' (San Blas, ~100 men) and a Sonora ship; Occidente replied (13 Feb) the brig 'Cosak' was readying at Mazatlán with 100 picked men under Capt. Eduardo García + 6–8,000 pesos & munitions; San Blas departure delayed, José de la Cruz ordered to expedite. ⭐ Immediate promotions to Alférez Manuel Gómez & José Estrada, who commanded the battery [Bouchard defense]

summary: Juan Salvador Aspiroz → Pedro Negrete: going to California with an expedition & staying a while, asks Negrete to send some rebozos, kimonos[?] etc. (Asian/Pacific goods)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 854, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 200–201 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n199–n200)

author: Mondragón
summary: Brígida Solá → Don Pablo Vicente Solá (his niece, Basque Country): family news — her aunt the nun sent word; they went to Madrid; her sister Joaquina married the *guardia* Joaquín (brother of 'Pepe'); a 'Canido[?]' who lived w/ Solá in Madrid gave news; hears he likes the guitar; begs him to send 'alguna cosita' — she's the only unmarried one, poor; her mother has died
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 856–857, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 201–202 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n200–n201)

date_text: 1817-02-29 [⚠ impossible — 1817 not a leap year; Savage error]
author: Mondragón
summary: Brígida Solá → Pablo V. Solá (2nd letter, much repeated): again begs 'alguna cosita,' fears ending an 'old maid' like her poor aunts; her mother died a month ago; signs Brígida Solá y Ceizaga[?]
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 858–859, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 202–203 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n201–n202)

author: Monterey
summary: María Luisa & Fernando → Ignacio de Acedo[?]: that Don Eduardo[?] & Don Antonio Fernández lodged in their house, arrived on the Mexican frigate with the expedition
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 860–861, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 203 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n202)

author: Loreto
summary: Certificate by José Darío Argüello (Gov. Baja Calif.): Santiago Smith Wilcocks, capt./owner of the schooner 'Caminante,' appeared at Loreto 3 Apr w/ a passport from the Gov. of Alta Calif. (25 Feb), and provisioned the starving Loreto presidio — 126 fanegas maize, 20 of beans (+ other goods), for which he was paid. Certified copy by José M.ª Estudillo, Monterey 12 Jun 1817
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 864, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 204 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n203)

author: Loreto
summary: José Darío Argüello → Solá: the Guadalajara cajas barely suffice ('vamos pasando esta triste vida llena de congojas'); on the seizure of Wilcocks's schooner 'Caminante' — nothing resolved, but captor Ramírez extracted goods so all his property is embargoed; Ramírez likely tangled it at the Provincias Internas command; Argüello has told the Viceroy of Wilcocks's good services in both Californias
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. ~865, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 205 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n204)

author: Monterey
summary: Lt. Yakov Podushkin (RAC) → Gov. Solá (English translation): requests the arrest & return of a Kodiak Aleut sailor, Peter Leonoff, of the schooner 'Chirikoff,' who deserted on 30 March from the port of 'Little Bodega' — to be forwarded to Novo-Arkhangelsk or Ross. = expanded Document 20
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 868, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 206 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n205)

author: RAC diplomatic protest — Alexander Baranov (Gov.-Gen. of the Russian American Possessions, Collegiate Counsellor, Knight of St. Anne 2nd Cl.)
recipient: Gov. Solá: protests 'insults to the Russian flag and the capture and keeping in cruel bondage of Russians and other people subject to our august Monarch… in the waters and coasts of California,' invoking the treaty of 1812 (arts. 3 & 4); has petitioned St. Petersburg / the Emperor; sends Lt. Yakov Podushkin aboard the *Chirikoff* as a *parlamentario*; closes 'The Holy Protector of California preserve you.' Translated by Ivan Petroff (i.e. for the Bancroft project, not 1817). = expanded Document 20

summary: original (Eng. transl. Petroff)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 866–870, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 207–209 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n206–n208)

cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 865–870, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 210 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n209)

author: aboard the *Bordelais*
summary: Camille de Roquefeuil → Gov. Solá (French): transmits a letter from M. Carvencia of Lima; forced to put in at San Francisco; asks Solá's protection for his ship; bases his confidence on the friendship between the two nations and 'the proofs the French gave of their sentiments toward the Spanish in the recent events in Chile'; Luis Argüello to forward two cases of French products as a gift. Signed 'De Roquefeuil, lieut. des vaisseaux du Roi'
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 871–872, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 211–212 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n210–n211)

author: San Francisco
summary: Manuel Gómez → Gov. Solá: on whether he may leave his post (Subinspector consulted; Viceroy's ruling); defends the cartridges he's charged with — not badly made, but of *bayeta* (baize), the proper material, made on his order
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 873–880, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 212 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n211)

summary: Gov. Solá → Luis Argüello: re buying from the RAC frigate 'Kutusoff' (cmdr. Hagemeister) — it has many goods; deal to buy ~$25,000[?] on draft against the *habilitación general*, goods for the troops & families of the four presidios at fair prices; ⭐ but the Kodiaks the frigate wants to take back are only four (some at Sta Bárbara, others at San Gabriel), some now Christian, too distant to arrive before it sails
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 884, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 212–213 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n211–n212)

summary: Gov. Solá → Cmdt. Hagemeister: very well disposed toward him & his Emperor; cannot deliver the Kodiaks before his departure (ill/far off) — will return them at first opportunity to Baranov; authorizes Lt. Argüello to buy $25,000 of goods for the four presidios on draft against the Guadalajara habilitado-general
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 881–882, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 213–214 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n212–n213)

summary: Solá → Luis Argüello: repeats the order to buy goods [from the *Kutusoff*], draw drafts, & notify him at once
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 882, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 214 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n213)

summary: Solá → Luis Argüello: reprimands his 'poca actividad y celo' — it pains him to remind a man of talent so often of the exactitude & vigilance required when a foreign ship comes to that port [SF]; handle the sale & purchase shrewdly
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 882–883, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 214–215 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n213–n214)

author: Monterey
summary: Solá → Luis Argüello: demands reports on the foreign ships maneuvering at SF (whether sailed or still there) and the proceeds of goods sold/produce extracted; displeased Argüello hasn't reported; notes (via Fr. Marcelino Marquínez) that Argüello dispatched an expedition — wants its motive/result
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 883–884, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 216–217 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n215–n216)

author: Monterey
summary: Inventory of the effects of Don Boris Tarasov & the 'Russian Indians' [Aleuts], taken at the Ensenada de San Pedro and returned by the governor's order to Lt. Jacobo (Yakov) Podushkin: a sack of rice, 10½ v. purple ribbon, 6 small bags of otter [pelts], 9 sea-lion skins, 12 gut-shirts (*camisas de tripa* = Aleut kamleikas), fishing instruments, lead, 9 badly-damaged muskets, Boris's notes, tools; note that tobacco/*bayetón*/a field-tent were consumed feeding the returning Aleuts; signed Monterey 5 May 1817 '(aquí hay varias palabras en idioma ruso).' [= the Mathes 'Tarasov effects-lists'; cf. Doc 99, Document 20]
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 884, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 217–218 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n216–n217)

author: Monterey
summary: Seizure inventory of Tarasov's & the Aleuts' effects — from Sgt. Carlos Carrillo, captured at the Ensenada de San Pedro from 'the diver called Boris, with twelve cayucos': 3 sacks rice, 2 tobacco, *bayetón*, purple China ribbon, blue cloth; ⭐ 2 small bags + 40 otter pelts (*pieles de Nutria*), 5 sea-lion skins, 12 gut-shirts (kamleikas), fishing gear, lead, 9 badly-damaged muskets (one barrel burst, most locks useless), powder, a field-tent, Boris's notebook, hammer/tongs/augers, an empty bottle. (capture-side list; cf. Doc 273; Mathes 'Tarasov effects-lists')
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 885–886, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 218–219 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n217–n218)

summary: Savage's note: ff. 888–895 are a duplicate of the judicial disposition on Coronel Arrillaga's testamentaría (already at folio 198 = catalog Doc 255) — no new content
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 888–895, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 219 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n218)

author: México
summary: Apodaca → Gov. Solá: the British frigate 'Buena Esperanza,' from Bengal with cargo for the Russian establishments (NW coast & Sandwich Islands), put in at Mazatlán (water/provisions, mainmast repair, sick crew); orders Capt. Silvestre Ramsay[?] to leave at once once repaired (fair prices), not to touch any other Spanish port on pain of confiscation; point-commanders to enforce *comiso*
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 996–1000, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 220–221 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n219–n220)

author: Arispe
summary: Antonio Cordero → Gov. Solá: the brig 'Cosak' at Guaymas — tried to water, threatened with sinking for lacking a port-captain; its Capt. Clark[?] jailed; the brig then set sail, raised the Anglo-American flag, fired 3 cannon-shots & fled (with abuse/improperios); orders it seized wherever it arrives, anyone landing arrested, goods confiscated
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1001–1004, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 221 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n220)

author: Arispe
summary: Antonio Cordero → Gov. Solá: the intendancy (31 Dec) condemned Wilcocks's schooner 'Caminante,' its cargo & all belonging to Santiago Smith [Wilcocks] & 'Sirca[?]' as forfeit (*decomiso*); orders Solá to embargo anything of theirs in his ports (closes the Wilcocks legal case; cf. Document 19)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1005–1006, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 222 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n221)

author: Guadalajara
summary: Gervasio Argüello → Gov. Solá: posted the bond the *Hacedor* demanded (guarantor Matías Vergara, on condition the money be kept in his house); still gets no *socorro* for Calif. (penury of the Real Cajas)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1007–1008, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 222 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n221)

author: Guadalajara
summary: Gervasio Argüello → Solá: transcribes the Viceroy's order on the bond obligation — if he can't post it, the Governor should name another habilitado
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1009–1010, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 223 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n222)

author: Guadalajara
summary: Gervasio Argüello → Solá: cannot receive *socorros* until the bond obstacle is cleared; resents being blamed for the delays; still seeking a hard-to-find guarantor; sends the *libranza*
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1011–1012, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 223 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n222)

author: Guadalajara
summary: Gervasio Argüello → Solá: inserts a royal order to the Mexico treasury to send the Real Cajas the revista extracts 1810–1814 of the Alta Calif. troops so their back-pay can be paid
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1013–1014, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 224 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n223)

author: San Antonio
summary: Carlos Antonio Carrillo → Gov. Solá: operations vs. the rebels [Bouchard] — arrived with 20 armed vecinos (2 muskets, 14 lances, 3 sabres, pistols); the enemy descended on Mission San Luis [Obispo] to attack it; he plans to go to its aid
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1015–1016, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 224 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n223)

author: San Francisco
summary: Luis Argüello → Gov. Solá: sends the 4 Christian Indians of Mission San Francisco — Teocoy[?], Félix, Nájara, Crescencio — culprits in the murder of Tobías & Norato; a revenge killing (the victims had slain Crescencio's brother); the two were surprised sleeping 4 leagues from San José — one beaten to death, one hanged, bound, stones at the neck, thrown in a deep pool; divers recovered the body
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1018–1022, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 224–225 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n223–n224)

author: San Isidro
summary: José de la Guerra → Gov. Solá: the enemy [Bouchard] sailed from the Ensenada del Refugio toward [Sta Bárbara] after burning & robbing the Ortega/Refugio rancho; ship-sighting reports; can't get Monterey's help; 'no tiene artillería útil ni gente; hará la defensa que pueda'; recalled the Monterey relief; if the rebels don't quit the coast he'll attack them where they land
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1023–1029, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 225–227 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n224–n226)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: Guerra → Solá: amid the meat shortage for the troops & families, takes the tithe cattle (from the Father President) on the company's account; asks Purísima's site 'Las Cañadas' (only during the calamitous times, until the presidio gets 2 yrs of memorias); already there with 672 head tended by 3 soldiers
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1031–1033, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 227 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n226)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: Guerra → Solá: on an expedition to recover fugitive mission Indians (*cimarrones*) — needs >25 days, best in Sept/Oct or harvest (Jun/Jul); the fugitives shelter on an islet 'Trapui[?]' ~70 leagues NE, surrounded by great lakes (*lagunas*), unreachable without boats — the refuge of most of the region's *cimarrones*; recommends night marches, 30 men from there + San Diego, trusted Indian scouts ahead
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1035–1039, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 228 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n227)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: Guerra → Solá: on withdrawing the invalids & service auxiliaries from escort duty; asks whether the vaqueros & Indian auxiliaries should also retire; mission Indians to help with the night guard at the rancho to avoid a surprise
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1040–1041, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 229 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n228)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: Guerra → Solá: received the soldier José Antonio Romero, sentenced to 6 months public works; will enforce the sentence
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1042–1043, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 229 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n228)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: Guerra → Solá: sends a reinforcement — Lt. Ignacio Martínez setting out at 8 AM with whatever people he can gather (Indians, non-capital prisoners offered the King's pardon if they fight with honor); ⭐ many unarmed (only fine cavalry muskets here; can be fitted with pikes/lances, 'la mejor arma' for them); 'yo quedo sin ninguna… el Señor no tiene atadas las manos; venceremos con su auxilio'
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1044–1045, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 229–230 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n228–n229)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: Guerra → Solá: given the critical circumstances, divested himself of the *habilitación*, handing it provisionally to Alférez Maytorena (to focus on defense)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1046+, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 230 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n229)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: Guerra → Solá: the two rebel [Bouchard] frigates left the presidio anchorage at dawn, vanishing from sight; sent reinforcement to Los Ángeles and 24 soldiers under Carrillo to San Diego
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1047–1048, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 231 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n230)

author: Rancho de la Real Hacienda
summary: Gov. Solá → the Fathers from San Luis to San Diego (circular): the rebels [Bouchard] hold the Monterey establishment/beach without daring to approach Mission San Carlos; yesterday set fire to the Castillo & Presidio [of Monterey]; keep lookouts, relay their course. ⭐ Followed by the missions' acknowledgment-relay chain with timestamps — Purísima (Fr. Mariano Payeras), Sta Inés (Fr. Francisco Javier Vara), San Buenaventura (José Ruiz), San Fernando (Fr. Marcos A. de Vitoria), San Gabriel (Fr. Joaquín Nuez), San Juan Capistrano (Fr. Gerónimo Boscana), San Luis Rey (Fr. Jaime Escudé) — the coastal warning network in action, 28–30 Nov 1818
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1049–1051, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 231–233 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n230–n232)

author: Monterey
summary: Solá → the commandants of Sta Bárbara & San Diego: the season being advanced (less risk the rebel ships will strike), withdraw the invalids & vecinos to their planting/homes, cover the points with the regular garrisons; keep vigilance; missions to post vaqueros. (Dated before the raid actually hit Monterey ~20–24 Nov)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1052–1054, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 233–234 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n232–n233)

author: Loreto
summary: José Darío Argüello → Gov. Solá: forwards the representation of the American corvette 'Mercurio' (the subject sought not in his jurisdiction); sends the *diligencias* for Solá to comply with the superior order (late follow-up on the 1813–14 *Mercurio* prize, Docs 101–102)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1055–1056, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 234 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n233)

author: San Francisco
summary: Luis Argüello → Gov. Solá: complains Solá doesn't write; Gabriel Moraga has marched from the presidio; four cannons placed at the most advantageous points, their esplanades being built
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1057–1059, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 235 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n234)

author: Monterey
summary: José M.ª Estudillo → Gov. Solá: on arms-making & fortification + the rebel [Bouchard] destruction at Monterey — repairing the muskets; approves making machetes to arm the company + sword-scabbards/belts; has mounted the 3 cannons & the esplanade, about to make grapeshot bags (*sacos de metralla*); on the Sta Cruz events sent the Alférez, Sergeant & others; ⭐ 'da compasión ver la madera y la teja' — and a wrecked house (only the oven-rooms left, orchard fence smashed, peach trees stripped)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1060–1061, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 235–236 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n234–n235)

date_text: 1819-08-17 [⚠ '1818' in some refs; content matches the 1819 *Cosak* voyage]
author: Monterey
summary: José M.ª Estudillo → Gov. Solá: the scarcity of funds at the Guadalajara cajas; the purchase Pablo de la Portilla brought (arrived at the San Luis ensenada) won't reach San Diego under a month (≥120 leagues, bad waterless country); the brig *Cosak* if it stays will have abundant fish for the crew
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1062–1064, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 236–237 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n235–n236)

author: Monterey
summary: José M.ª Estudillo → Gov. Solá: Buitrón arrived with 'la presa' (the captives) — 37 women & children held at El Carmelo (+ some orphans given to live there); the captives kept from the presidio so the Indian men, seeing their wives & families, won't flee; he is building the furnaces for red-hot shot (*hornillos para la bala roja*)
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1065–1066, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 237 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n236)

author: Monterey
summary: José M.ª Estudillo → Gov. Solá: on the state of the batteries — of the cannons the [rebels] burst, found 3 that, mounted at once, could serve as a parapet; has mounted them; requested the 3 cannons SF left
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1067–1068, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 238 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n237)

author: Monterey
summary: Estudillo → Solá: on the events of 22 Nov [the Bouchard attack on Monterey]; doubts the efficacy of the Viceroy's measures; beginning the timber-cut; needs workers 'para levantar las ruinas'
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1069–1071, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 238 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n237)

author: Monterey
summary: Estudillo → Solá: copied the four royal orders of 4 Apr 1818, 12 Jun, etc.
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1072–1073, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 239 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n238)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: José de la Guerra → Solá: Colorado-Indian attack at Mission San Buenaventura — 20 Colorado Indians came, repelled by the guard (Cabo Fuentes); during Mass the rebels seized muskets, killing a corporal & a servant; 12 soldiers + a sergeant w/ a cannon sent in pursuit. [→ mil-history register; cf. Doc 78, Document 11]
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1074–1076, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 239 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n238)

summary: Gabriel Moraga → Gov. Solá: expedition against the Amajava (Mojave) — set out with 50 men + 10 vecinos eastward; reached Mongarayait[?]/Agallaga (last pasture, 27 horses lost), carried water in vessels, went inland; a gentile Indian killed one of his boys (to rob his horse & blanket). [= expanded Document 11]
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1077–1081, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 239–210[?] (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n238–n239)

author: Santa Bárbara
summary: Gabriel Moraga → Gov. Solá: forwards reports from the San Gabriel & San Fernando escorts on the Amajaba (Mojave) Indians' intentions; warns to live with great caution
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1082–1083, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 210[?] (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n239)

author: San Gabriel
summary: Hilario Machado → the commandants up to Sta Bárbara: warning of the Mojave (Amajaba) approach — the Indian corporal of Sumibabi (18 lgs E) reported 20 gentile Indians of San Sebastián relating that an escaped captive among the Amajabas faithfully warned the Mojaves had set out toward these missions 'a pelear y a hacer el daño posible'. [= expanded Document 11; indigenous-intel]
cite: Provincial State Papers, MS, tom. XX, p. 1084–1085, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 13, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 241 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n240)

author: San Blas

summary: Instructions for the relief-expedition ships 'San Carlos' (war-brig) & 'Reina de los Ángeles' (armed merchant frigate) — to relieve Alta Calif. summary: Gov. Solá → the presidio commandants — the foundational Bouchard-defense circular + full mobilization/evacuation *ordenanza* (signed Monterey 8 Oct 1818). Warning (via Guerra, from an American ship): 2 pirate frigates (34 guns / 18–20 guns, 350 men) left the Sandwich Islands, bound for this coast in 4–6 days. Plan: secure all church silver/gold to named inland depots (SF→San José; Monterey→Soledad; San Luis→Sta Margarita; Purísima→San Antonio rancho; SD→San Antonio de Pala…); cache provisions; evacuate women & children; drive cattle & horse-herds inland; muster discharged men & invalids (Luis Argüello at SF; Ortega & Mariano Castro ranchos); a flying squad w/ 300-cartridge reserve; disperse 2/3 of the powder inland; ⭐ spike the cannons if abandoned; double mounted-Indian lookouts; ⭐⭐ a statewide mounted-courier relay route (SF→San Mateo→San José→Castro's rancho→Monterey→Soledad→San Antonio→San Miguel→San Luis→Purísima→Sta Inés→Sta Bárbara→San Buenaventura…, relay-padres Oliva/Cabot/Ripoll/Sánchez); free the prisoners for service; Guerra named 2nd-in-command of arms / accidental governor if Solá falls. = expanded Document 21

author: Tte. José Francisco de Ortega, Comte. of San Diego
themes: indigenous-resistance; missions; san-diego; san-juan-capistrano; martyrdom; 1775-revolt; anza
summary: Primary account of the 4–5 Nov 1775 San Diego Mission revolt & killing of Fr. Luis Jayme. *Expediente de investigación* on the burning of Mission San Diego & death of a missionary. Narrative: 2 Oct, Frs. Luis Jayme & Vicente Fuster let their Indians go fishing; the brothers Francisco & Carlos (Carlos = mission 'capitán') robbed old gentile women of fish at rancho de la Chiapa (2 lgs.); the women complained; thieves fled night of the 5th; 5 principal SD-ranchería Indians seized. Night of 5 Nov: gentiles of the Sierra + various Christians attacked at midnight, burned the church, the Fathers' houses & the guard, and killed Fr. Luis Jayme (found at dawn near the arroyo, stripped, riddled with arrows, head & face smashed). Casualties: carpenter Maestro [José] Urselino mortally wounded (2 arrows, died the 10th); mason Manuel Arroyo killed (body burned); mason Felipe Romero wounded but killed an Indian & held out with the guard; 4 escort soldiers gravely wounded (cabo Rocha[?]; Alejo Antonio Gonzáles, Juan Álvarez, Joaquín Armenta); soldiers Ignacio Vallejo[?], Anastasio Camacho, Juan de Ortega singled out for valor. Christian rancherías in the attack: San Luis, Matamó[?], Tamacha[?], Meté, Yana, Abacaly[?] & newly reduced San Miguel; gentile rancherías Melojó[?], Itai, Pocol, El Corral + ~6 more from the San Luis cañada. Defense: earthwork thrown up around the missionaries' houses; sergeant + 10 soldiers raided ranchería Janat[?] on the 24th seeking ringleader Rafael (not found) but seized a principal cabecilla, 12 women & 3 children + recovered church effects; Christian Indian Joaquín & capitán Mariano Yguatín[?] (rancho de Aguacal[?]) examined — rancherías planned a dawn attack on the presidio within 20 days, 'kill the Padres & soldiers but not the women,' allies from across the Colorado River ('tierras libres' boast). Ortega (27 Nov) asked Anza for 20 men. Certified copy by Capt. Fernando de Rivera y Moncada; original sent to the Viceroy of México. Orig. pp.~1–34 [cite at n8 partly illeg.; Doc 2 begins at orig. p.35].
cite: Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military), MS, p. 1–7, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 15, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 2–9 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n2–n8)

José [Joaquín] Moraga, Sargto Pablo Grijalva, 5 cabos (Domingo Alviso, Valerio Mesa, Pablo Pinto, Gabriel Peralta; Ramón Reforgera[?]/Bojorques almacenero), 33 soldados (Amézquita, Pacheco, Linares, Soto, Valencia, Bojorques, Joaquín de Castro, Felipe Tapia, Juan Fco. Bernal, Santiago Pico, Cordero, Galindo, Silvas, Peralta, Sebastián López, Vicente Félix…) = 1 Tte, 1 Sargto, 5 cabos, 33 soldados. Plus pobladores, sirvientes of the presidio & of Missions SF & Sta Clara, 4 misioneros (Frs. Palóu, Cambón, Murguía, de la Peña). Pay: Tte $700, Sargto $450, cabo $400, soldado $365; pobladores/sirvientes $120/yr + rations. Rations (no meat issued — meat was hunted): flour, maíz, frijol, lenteja, garbanzo, arroz, manteca, panocha, chile. Total company wages for the year $14,795; owed to 28 men $7,223 + 8 soldiers $549; the 5 cabos posted out (Alviso→Presidio, Mesa→Pueblo San José, Pinto→Presidio, Peralta→Sta Clara, Bojorques→Mission SF). Early SF founding-generation roster — genealogically rich. Orig. pp.35–200.

summary: Criminal causa — death of an India at San Gabriel. Witnesses (4–6 Oct): cabo Olivera, alcalde Juan Diego Verdugo, alférez-indio Nicolás, indio Matías, indio Ignacio María (accuser), Avelia[?] (the accused's mother). Nothing appeared against the accused — the accuser had borne false witness; Ortega ordered the false accuser jailed & given 35 lashes over 3 days, with a warning to be far slower to accuse, 'y mucho más en asuntos criminales.' themes: indigenous-resistance; missions; san-diego; execution; justice; 1775-revolt; pamó
summary: The Pamó conspiracy & firing-squad execution of 4 Indian captains. On 16 Mar, Benito, an Indian capitán, warned (via Fr. Lasuén) that the Indians of Pamó — esp. their capitán Aarán[?] — were gathering arms to kill Christians; 3 neighbouring captains + others 'del otro lado de la sierra' were in the plot, which had killed a fugitive from San Juan Capistrano. Aarán defied Ortega, daring the soldiers to come 'para cogerlos á mano y matarlos á macanazos.' Sargto Mariano Carrillo (+ cabo, 8 soldiers, 2 guides) surprised Pamó at 3am on 31 Mar; the captains were seized & bound; 2 Indians killed, a few burned in a house refusing to surrender; the rest submitted & were flogged. >1,500 arrows, 80+ bows & many war-clubs taken & burned. The 4 captains — Achil, Aalcuirin[?], Aarán, Taguaqui[?] — examined 4 Apr, convicted of conspiring to kill the Christians despite a royal pardon, 'por haber juntado gente… para pelear con los de la Soledad después de la destrucción de la Misión' [1775 SD revolt]. ⚠️ Ortega's sentence (verbatim): 'los condeno á que el día 11 á las 9 de la mañana mueran con la violencia de dos tiros de escopeta, presente la tropa armada en guerra, y todas las rancherías cristianas… para que les sirva de estímulo á obrar bien.' And to the friars (re baptism): 'si se reducen á las aguas del Santo Bautismo, mueran el Sábado 11… por la mañana, y si no, también.' Lasuén began instructing them; the condemned disposed to be baptized. (Savage notes a discrepancy in the certified copy.) Orig. pp.737–764, 767–769.
cite: Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military), MS, p. 737–764, 767–769, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 15, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 43–46 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n42–n45)

summary: Memorandum on the presidial horse-herd situados (caballadas) & frontier cavalry doctrine. Argues the heavy company situado (346 horses, 67 mules) is unsustainable & self-defeating: constant field service ruins the soldier's kit & indebts him, leaves no time for drill, the penal law, religion, or to see wife & children — 'un hombre hambriento que lleva una vida miserable y abandonada.' The Apaches 'buscan siempre apoderarse de caballos y mulas'; once robbed, the troops are left 'á pie' and 'cesan sus operaciones por muchos meses.' Remedy: reduce each soldier to 2 horses + 1 mule kept stable-fed (caballerizas). Company effective strength: 71 plazas → 61 effective (guardia de caballada 20, escolta de prisiones/caudales 15, correos/enfermos/presos 8 → 21 left). Copia legalizada by Cap. Bonilla. Orig. pp.9–44 (vide pp.12–14).

summary: On the disadvantages of the large caballada situado & the rising military parity of the frontier Indians. Forwards his memo on the drawbacks of horse-herd situados (vide pp.3–9) for opinion; argues a California soldier needs fewer than 7 horses + 1 mule given his lighter fatigues vs. Sonora. Striking verbatim passage: when the enemy Indians were first encountered they 'ignoraban el uso de nuestros caballos y armas' and 2 soldiers could rout hundreds — but now 'todos los indios bárbaros que nos hacen la guerra saben ya el uso del arma de fuego, y algunas naciones la poseen con más acierto y seguridad que nuestras tropas mal disciplinadas, habiendo adelantado en el de sus flechas, lanzas y macanas'; they attack in equal numbers, dispute actions, rove the royal roads at will — 'se acabó el tiempo en que un pequeño número de nuestros soldados se hacía respetar de multitud de indios.' After 40 years of war the frontier costs the King >$804,000/year. Closes: ceasing horse/mule breeding in California & the frontier provinces would deter foreigners from penetrating these dominions (they would lack transport across the intervening deserts). After detaching men to gather ore, the camp (real) was attacked from the rear by 60+ Indians; the sergeant fought back wounding several but could not reach camp, found it in ruins; soldiers Gabriel Espinosa & Ignacio Carlón were killed (Carlón slain asleep; Espinosa made a vigorous defense), weapons (espadas, mangas, escopetas) seized. author: Manuel Merino (asesor's opinion)
summary: Opinion on the New California poblador livestock-grant policy & the tithe/cattle-disposal dispute. Each settler was given (as ventajas or 'por poblador') 2 mares, 2 cows with a calf, 2 ewes & 2 goats, to graze together & breed for 2 years (no killing or selling), then to build to 15 mares + a stallion, 15 cows + a bull, 12 ewes + a ram, 10 nanny-goats + a billy. Debates whether settlers retain the old liberty to dispose of their stock (the tithe-holders would limit it); concludes only male animals may be culled as needed, the Government guarding against abuses. summary: Investigation into the 1799 capture of the Spanish sloop *Mercedes* by a British squadron in the Gulf of California (Anglo-Spanish War). *See expanded Entry A below.* The balandra *Mercedes* (Bernardo Suárez), San Blas→Guaymas with country produce + passengers (José Gonzáles, Cristóbal Salas, 9 Guainamota Indians for the Islas Marías carey/turtle-shell fishery), found English traces at the Marías (cut wood, salt taken, a barraca, papers in English ink, English gunflints), then boarded & seized by an English frigate (29–31 May). The 'Presidente de la escuadra' claimed a fleet of frigates detached from Cabo San Lucas hunting the ship that left San Blas 20 May and awaiting the Manila galleon ('la nao de China'); they had a fortified sick-camp with cannon on San Juanito island; refused a $1,000 ransom, taking instead cattle/onions/hens + sugar, chocolate, panocha, a bell, etc. transferred from the prize. Named ships/captains: frigate 'Tester' [Vesta?] 18 guns + 14 carronades, Cmdt. Clark[?] (squadron chief); frigate 'Net-siut' 24/16 guns, Capt. Moss[?]/Moore; frigate 'Viñas' [Venus?] 18 guns; 'Pájaro' [Bird] 14 guns, Capt. Powell[?] (who had flown American colors at Banderas valley). They claimed 22 prizes off Peru (incl. a 12-gun brig at Paita) & to have robbed the warehouses of Sonsonate. Bombshell close: they did not fear San Blas even with 60 cannon, might raid it on their December retreat, and planned to winter at San Diego — 'instruidos por los planos de [Clower?] de Nutka' and carrying men who two years prior [c.1797] in two frigates near San Diego had, one moonlit night, entered in their boats, sounded the whole harbour, and knew its approaches.' summary: State & needed reinforcement of the California presidios — response to the Viceroy's order to fortify against British ships & to occupy Bodega Bay. Acknowledges the Viceroy's order (24 Nov 1792) to put the new establishments 'en el posible mejor estado de defensa, por si algo de los buques ingleses que hoy cruzan esta costa arribasen… para que no observen nuestra debilidad,' and a second order resolving to occupy the puerto de la Bodega and fortify San Francisco, Monterey & San Diego. Reports the artillery state (SF 2 cannon, both unserviceable; Monterey 8 + 3 pedreros good; SB 2 + 1 pedrero; SD 3, dismounted/no gunners) and that the guard is 'imaginaria.' Proposes garrisons: SD 75, Monterey 75, SB 63, SF 51; a small San Blas schooner at Monterey & SF Oct–Apr; 'y si se ocupa la Bodega se necesitará una fuerza por eso.' Orig. pp.72–78.

They declared they had deserted 'del establecimiento ruso… más arriba de Bodega' (Fort Ross) for the great hunger there; that there was no ship but one beached; *'que su Comandante Coscof [Kuskov] trabaja de duro en fábrica; que ya tienen cuatro casas grandes; pero no saben… cuál será el motivo de establecerse allí.'* Primary account of Fort Ross's first months. author: José Cavenecia (capt./owner of the *Eagle*)
recipient: Gob. José Argüello; *diligencias* by Tte. José Mª Estudillo
themes: russia; america; astor; fort-ross; bodega; foreign-relations; ships; britain
summary: Capture of the American brig *Pedler* by the Spanish-chartered frigate *Eagle* in the ensenada de San Luis Obispo (26 Aug 1814). Cavenecia lured the *Pedler* by raising the U.S. flag, then hoisted the Spanish, fired 2 cannon-shots & boarded with 25 men. Papers seized: U.S. govt passport, property register, crew roll, accounts, a Russian passport from Nuevo Arcángel (Sitka) signed by Gen. Baranov, the cargo manifest & a drawing made aboard. Commander = Mr. Wilson P. Hunt (the Astorian / Pacific Fur Co.). Depositions: the *Pedler* came from Bodega, had carried Sandwich Islands goods for the Russian establishment, left some at Bodega, and sought the Russian brig *María* (alias *Lev*); pilot Gilbert Cárdenas[?] had loaded at Columbia [River] goods from 'el Gral. Ruso Granoff' for Bodega. Cargo inventory (Estudillo, 7 Sep): porcelain, glassware, sugar, coffee, beads, Russian wool, colored thread, painted cloth, shirts, pants, furs, hats, etc. Argüello (9 Sep) — since the *Pedler* truly sought the *María* to deliver the cargo, orders the captor to set sail and leave these coasts with cargo & papers. ⭐ Exposes the Baranov/RAC–Astor (Hunt) Pacific supply network through Bodega/Fort Ross. Orig. pp.197–219
cite: Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military), MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 17, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 107–110 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n106–n109)

summary: Long *borrador* register of Solá's outgoing letters/orders (1815–1822) — a major composite source. 1815–17 highlights: ⭐⭐⭐ the 5 neophyte murderers of Fr. Andrés Quintana (Lino, Antonino, Vicente, Saturnino & Fulgencio[?] of Sta Cruz) sentenced (10 Mar 1816) to 200 azotes + presidio (10 yrs the first two, 7 the others), at Sta Bárbara — resolution of the Quintana murder (cf. Doc 153); ⭐⭐ Solá commissions Gabriel Moraga, 25 men, to reconnoiter the sierra passes (18 Oct 1816); ⭐ a 3-masted brig built at San Juan Capistrano (Capt. Guillermo/William Reynolds); *cimarrón* pursuit & a San Gabriel uprising; SD soldiers Franco/Fermín/Fernando tried for the homicide of the Mayordomo Miguel; Vicente Nevado poisoning his wife; José Antº Tapia raping a neophyte; warship *San Carlos* + corbeta *Paz y Religión*; request for 40 mission Indians. 1819–20 highlights (the post-Bouchard reinforcement & Moraga's Mojave campaign): ⭐⭐ arrival at San Luis of the Mazatlán company — brig *Cossack* w/ 100 men + $10,000, Capt. Pablo de la Portilla (+ corbeta *Reina de los Ángeles*, *San Carlos*); promotions: Mariano Estrada (Tte.) & Manuel Gómez (artillery); ⭐⭐ Solá orders Gabriel Moraga's 1819 punitive campaign to the Mojave (Amajabat/Mongallune) ranchería — 35 cavalry + 15 Mazatlán infantry under Tte. Narciso Fabregat 'para conocer á los gentiles la bravura de las armas del Rey' (revenge-raids by Colorado-River gentiles had hit San Buenaventura, taking 5 Christian captives); ⭐ Moraga couldn't reach Amajabat for lack of pasture, halting at San Joaquín & Santa Ana de Aguablanca, returning via San Gabriel (Antonio Mª Lugo alcalde); to resume next summer. 1820–21 highlights: ⭐ English whaler at the coast (Aug 1820, 36 crew, 200 barrels whale oil, 'fragata inglesa ballenera,' Capt. Guillermo [William] —; her captain caroused with Capt. Francisco Mª Ruiz, who was removed from the SD command/habilitación 'por el uso de ciertos licores', replaced by José Mª Estudillo); foreigner-vigilance warnings; ⭐⭐ death of Cadet José Guadalupe Moraga at San Gabriel (Mar 1821); the Cocomaricopa 'general' sent home in peace (the gentiles hostile at San Buenaventura 2 yrs prior); murder of the Mazatlán soldier Pablo Serna & the neophyte Apolonia; continued Amajaba/Mojave alarms (gentiles plotting to draw off the Christians of San Gabriel & San Fernando); Estudillo's 40-yr service/seniority dispute; ⭐ the American schooner *Eagle* suspected of clandestine trade (Fabregat sold it goods — foreign commerce prohibited); the Cocomaricopa 'general' returned to his patria; command reshuffle (Ruiz→SD, Portilla→Sta Bárbara); ends w/ the death of Fr. Joaquín Pascual Nuez (San Gabriel, 1822). Orig. pp.152–350

summary: SECOND *borrador* register of Solá's outgoing orders (1815–17) — the volume's richest Russian/foreign-relations stretch. Indigenous/campaign: ⭐⭐ Moraga's 1815 Palomas expedition (Solá orders Comte. Luis Argüello to mount 50 men—35 presidial + 15 inválidos/vecinos—and Gabriel Moraga to direct from Santa Cruz the campaign to the Ranchería de las Palomas); ⭐⭐⭐ Solá's Russian-trade policy query ('cuántas veces los Rusos han entrado… qué se les ha suministrado, cómo lo han pagado,' whether to continue/cut communication 'con otros Rusos, Anglo-Americanos ú otra Nación extranjera'); the Quintana assassins causa remitted to Gómez (Lino, Antonio, Vicente, Julián, Ambrosio, Andrés, Secundino, Fulgencio); the Juan Eliot de Castro chest sequestered (RAC agent, cf. C-A 12); Sgt. Soto's expedition. Russian/foreign maritime (1816–17): ⭐⭐⭐⭐ Kotzebue's *Rurik* at SF (Oct 1816) — 'franquee todos los auxilios que necesite el buque de Nueva Rusia, su Comandante Kossebue [Kotzebue]… que ancló ayer'; ⭐⭐⭐ the Russian ship *Suvorov* ('Serraroff,' Lazarev) at SF (21 Aug); ⭐⭐⭐ two Russians fled from 'el establecimiento situado arriba del Puerto de Bodega' (Fort Ross), declarations taken (Nov 1816); ⭐⭐⭐ the Russian war-chief Podushkin + an 'almost-resolved' decision to hand him a packet from St. Petersburg (Mar 1817); ⭐⭐ an anchored Russian ship's request to leave canoes/baidarkas at Sausalito to hunt (denied); ⭐⭐ the French corvette *Bordelais* (Roquefeuil), 200 t, for wood & water (Aug 1817, took deserters); ⭐⭐ an English NWC brig from the Columbia River (Aug 1816); ⭐⭐ defensive measures vs. the 'insurgentes de Buenos Aires' (pre-Bouchard, 1816: spike the battery guns if taken, missions to ready bows & arrows); ⭐ Fort San Joaquín works concluded (Gómez). summary: Causa criminal — the poisoning of Fr. Pedro Panto by his Indian cook Nazario (Mission San Diego). Cabo Antonio Guillén & Sgt. Mariano Mercado noticed the friar's soup tasted bitter (16 Nov); Panto vomited badly. Nazario confessed he'd carried a poison herb ('escoba amarga') for days and put it in the soup because Panto flogged him relentlessly — by his account 50 + 24 + 25 + 25 lashes over 15–16 Nov (200+ in two days 'sin dar graves motivos') — 'por ver si de este modo descansaba yo y los demás indios de la Misión'; testified 'ningún indio de la Misión lo quiere, ni menos los gentiles; y al Padre Sánchez tanto lo quieren los cristianos como los gentiles.' Defensor Pico: the herb wasn't lethal, Nazario 'un indio bruto,' driven by desperation. Fiscal Carrillo finds him not deserving of execution — asks 8 months' presidio at San Diego 'para escarmiento de los demás.' A landmark primary source on mission corporal punishment & indigenous resistance. Orig. pp.101–29

themes: criminal; indigenous; missions; santa-cruz; quintana; resistance
summary: Causa criminal — the 1820 interrogation of the neophyte Alberto (Mission Sta Cruz) re the murder of Fr. Andrés Quintana. Alberto's sworn testimony: the Indian Quirico invited him 'á ayudar á matar al Padre,' luring him to the mission huerta at prayer-time on the pretext of stealing pears, where the other conspirators were gathered; the Indian Andrés confirmed they meant to kill the Padre; Alberto says he refused ('que él no se metía en nada'), left for home, learned next morning the Padre was dead; confessed he did wrong not to warn the guard/mayordomo; fled to the *Monte*/sierra when the others were arrested, fed once by his son via Fr. Marcelino, told to go to Punta de Año Nuevo (the mission rancho). A rich primary indigenous-testimony source on the Quintana assassination (cf. Docs 153/177/188). Orig. pp.707–10

summary: 'Declaraciones de insurgentes de la expedición de Bouchard' — depositions of the 4 captured/surrendered crew of Bouchard's frigates, revealing the multinational makeup of the expedition: (1) Pedro Saldívar, 22, of Buenos Aires, cabo; (2) Juan de la Rosa, 27, of Scotland, labrador; (3) Nicolás Blanco, 21, of Santa Fé, soldier of the frigate *Consecuencia*; (4) Mateo José Pascual, ~25, native of Africa, panadero, baptized in Buenos Aires. All questioned on Isidro Molina — uniformly testify he was drunk at the Monterey presidio, riding a white horse, not a prisoner, who came over voluntarily ('se ha venido á pasar á presentar'), with a rumor he was a spy (*vigía*) sent by the Governor; couldn't say if he landed at the Ortegas' rancho or went ashore willingly at Sta Bárbara. Each signed with a cross (illiterate). A remarkable primary source on Bouchard's crew & the Molina case. Orig. pp.~256–61

summary: Causa criminal — the neophyte Antonio/Rafael Chales flogged his wife María Gabriela to death (Mission San Diego). The escort cabo Pedro Lobo found her body whip-marked, 'de la cintura abajo, en los muslos, toda desollada, enseñando la carne viva.' summary: The Branciforte sack of Mission Santa Cruz during the Bouchard scare. Fr. Ramón Olbés complained the Branciforte comisionado & villagers committed 'atentados' on the mission's property. When Bouchard's force took Monterey (23 Nov 1818), Olbés evacuated the mission toward Sta Clara; the comisionado Joaquín Buelna had been ordered to remove the mission's goods (under inventory) before the enemy could sack them — instead, the inválido Joaquín Castro found Buelna & most of the Branciforte vecindario sacking the mission: forcing the main gate with axes, breaking the warehouse windows, carrying off the goods; returning 6–7 days later they found it 'enteramente saqueada,' doors/windows/stores broken, the church profaned — a crucifix, the image of San Luis & the Santo Niño 'hechos pedazos,' excrement on canes in the sacristy. A vivid, well-known episode. The testimony is conflicting: the comisionado Joaquín Buelna's defense quotes the Gov.'s actual written order ('hará V. que pase con algunos á destruir aquellos intereses para que los enemigos no se apoderen de ellos') and blames the mayordomo Castro & 60 mission Indians for the disorderly sack; villager José Mª Salazar says Castro broached the liquor barrels; some say the Indians (not the villagers) broke the crucifix and that San José/the Santo Niño were undamaged. Argüello sent all the declarations to the Gov. (18 Nov 1819). Orig. pp.3–26
cite: Provincial State Papers, Benicia (Military), MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 17, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 276–278+ (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n276–n278)

summary: Causa criminal — incest/rape by a stepfather (CLOSED). Per comisionado Manuel Rodríguez's report, Cornelio Rosales (of Branciforte; 41 años, natural de San Luis Obispo, casado con María Luisa Robles[?]) impregnated his stepdaughter María Antonia Sepúlveda and committed estupro on his goddaughter (hijada de bautismo) María Josefa; younger sisters María Paula & María Inés also implicated, the children sleeping together. Timoteo Vásquez offered to marry María Antonia & 'take the blame.' Conflicting careos: María Antonia & María Paula affirm Cornelio violated them; Rosales & María Josefa deny. Dictamen fiscal (Martínez): estupro 'plenamente justificado,' aggravated by mal ejemplo & público escándalo 'abriendo las puertas á muchos para que sigan sus maldades'; recommends Rosales removed from the Province — 4 años de trabajos públicos con grillete al pie at the presidio de San Diego. Penances for the girls (azotes by their mother's hand, in the girls' room at Mission Santa Cruz): María Josefa 50 azotes; María Antonia 50 azotes + 1 month arrest; Paulita 25 azotes; the mother a stern reprimand. Tied to the 'revolución de los insurgentes' (Bouchard period, Dec 1818) at Buena Vista rancho; midwife examinations confirmed abuse. Orig. pp.348–368.

'(No se encuentra la defensa)' — defense not in the record. Orig. pp.417–453.

summary: The longest expediente in the volume (~LXVI pp. 90–390, dragging from Aug 1828 into 1831). Causa criminal for the murder of two small children — María Antonia (~5 yrs) and Blas de Jesús (~1 yr), children of soldier Ignacio Olivas — and the estupro (rape) of the girl, on the denuncia of soldier Ignacio Ribas; accused: fellow SF-company soldier Francisco Rubis (25, native of Los Ángeles). Post-mortem autopsy 16 Aug 1828 by the English settler-physician Antonio [William A.] Richardson ('de nación inglés'): both children strangled with a cord, the girl raped. Evidence: parents at a fandango at Sra Bibiana's; a surviving small child blamed 'un coyote muy bravo'; Rubis (who had quarreled with the mother 4 days before) tried that night to swap a clean shirt and passed off a bloodstained *sarape* (borrowed from Juan García, returned via young Rafael Pacheco) — central evidence; Rubis claimed the blood was sheep's (de borrego). Procedural wrangling over jurisdiction, fiscal turnover (Mariano G. Vallejo among fiscals), and the Monterey↔SF distance. Fiscal Padrés (27 May 1831) recommended sparing Rubis the death penalty given time served; ⭐⭐⭐ but Rubis was EXECUTED by garrote, maintaining his innocence — and per an inserted eyewitness reminiscence of Ignacio Cibrián (b. 18 Oct 1816, SF; he was ~14 at the execution), ~2 years later an Indian arrested for robbery/murder, sentenced to death, confessed that *he* had committed the crime and that 'Rubis murió inocente' — a documented wrongful execution. (A Bancroft-collector's English note vouches: 'Cibrián is a man of family… very honorable… living in the rancho of Salsi Puedes, Contra Costa County, near Mount Diablo.') An early CA forensic examination + a wrongful-execution case
cite: Dep. State Papers, Benicia (Military), MS, tom. LXVI, p. ~90–390, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 18, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n327–n386)

summary: The Solís-revolt conspiracy sumaria (June–Aug 1829). Fernández del Campo reports (18–21 Jun) that cabo Mariano Vaquero[?], artilleryman Pablo/Pedro Guerrero[?] (Savage's copy writes 'Pablo' on the first leaf, 'Pedro' on the next) & cavalry-soldier Juan Lisalde[?] revealed a conspiracy 'que debía ser dirigida por el presidiario Sargto Solís' against the territorial chief (Echeandía) and all the officers, to put the offices 'en manos de hijos de la tierra.' The plan (a junta): seize the artillery cuartel, casa-mata, castillo & other key points of Monterey, assault set for the night of the 22nd. ⭐ Alférez M. G. Vallejo, asked to continue the sumaria (8 Jul), recused himself — because he was commanding the very company accused of the plot, and as habilitado; cadet Raymundo Estrada brought from SF (11 Aug) to continue, but Fernández del Campo declined to re-depose before him, and 'aquí queda truncado el asunto' (the investigation breaks off — Solís launched the actual revolt that November). summary: Measure to check the Russians of Ross/Bodega — the grant of 'Santa Rosa' as a barrier. Echeandía, holding it 'de suma importancia á la seguridad é integridad del territorio nacional,' resolves to plant a settlement on the land between Mission San Rafael and the Russian establishment of the puerto de Bodega, 'que sirva de barrera' against foreign incursion 'para posesionarse de él, como lo han hecho del que ocupan' (i.e., as the Russians did at Bodega) — prompted by the San Rafael missionary's fear (after a Russian reconnaissance the prior year) and to draw in the gentile Indians. He grants the tract known as Santa Rosa to the petitioner 'D.n R. Gómez' (✅ scan-verified 2026-07-01, n65 — first name abbreviated to the initial in Savage's copy; almost certainly the asesor Rafael Gómez, but the document gives only 'R.') (with powers for agriculture & stock-raising) under Art. 12 of the 18 Aug 1824 colonization decree, expressly provisional pending the Exma Diputación (likely never perfected — the 'Cabeza de Santa Rosa' grant went to María Ignacia López de Carrillo in 1841). (Borrador.) The Mexican continuation of Solá's 1818 San Rafael barrier strategy vs. Fort Ross. Orig. pp.166–167.

author: Romualdo Pacheco, Comandante
themes: solis-revolt; military-history; san-francisco; mutiny; artillery; russian-frigate; argüello; de-haro; piña; 1829
summary: 'Sublevación de Solís' — the Cabo Joaquín Piña salute causa. Pacheco orders Ramírez to open a sumaria on a complaint (relayed via art. cmdt. José Fernández del Campo from SF cmdt. Ignacio Martínez, dated 20 Feb) against artillery Cabo José Joaquín Piña. Martínez's account: on 28 Nov [1829] at 1 PM, while he was at home with his family (alférez Francisco de Haro present), Piña entered and demanded 'con mucha altanería y falta de respeto' five rounds 'para saludar á la expedición' [of Solís]; despite Martínez insisting only the 5 tiros (cal. 3) be taken, Piña and artillerymen Maldonado & [Pedro/Lucas] Soto hauled off a whole cajón of ammunition to the artillery cuartel and, 'poco después comenzaron á hacer el saludo al entrar la expedición de Solís, habiendo izado la bandera nacional al verificarlo.' Witness Eusebio Soto: they took the cajón 'con el fin de hacer salva á la exp[edició]n de Solís que iba entrando,' and Piña said 'que él quería ir con todos los artilleros á correr la misma suerte que su Comand.te y su hermano, que sabía se hallaban presos en Monterey.' Escribanos cadet Raymundo Estrada then Sebastián[?] Rodríguez. Joaquín Piña's own deposition (n81–85) adds: a Russian frigate lay in the bay (Martínez was aboard it on 28 Nov); Solís's salute protocol was 5 shots on entry, 5 when the plan was read, 5 when the troops withdrew to quarters; the SF plaza was effectively handed over to Solís ('antes de entregar la plaza'; the courier José Sánchez carried Martínez's surrender-reply); and Martínez, the late ex-Gov. Luis de Argüello, alf. Sánchez & Haro were seen reading & praising Solís's plan ('muy lindo y muy bueno… como los mandamientos de la ley de Dios'). Piña refused to muster, retorting he 'no era indio de conquista.' Savage notes the rest of the causa is not present and that Piña was commanding the SB artillery detachment 31 Dec 1830. → verbatim depositions in Expanded Entry A below. Orig. pp.452–475, 476.
cite: Dep. State Papers, Benicia (Military), MS, p. 452–476, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 19, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 78–85 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n78–n85)

summary: Orders a reserved sumaria into Alférez Domingo Carrillo's scandalous conduct one night at a fandango at the civilian Anastasio Leiva's house, where soldiers of his company had mixed in; Carrillo tried to march Cabo Juan Mª Marrón back to quarters, words passed, and the officer 'le prometió su venganza.' SD cmdt. reported it 5 Nov; Tte. Santiago Argüello opened the sumaria 10 Sept, escribano cadet Ignacio del Valle. Marrón's deposition: at ~11 PM, missing soldiers Ramón Sotelo & Esteban Higuera, he found them 'enfandangados' at Leiva's; Carrillo, 'un poco trastornado de la cabeza' from aguardiente, fronted him — 'Sí, sí, váyase pronto, porque si no, lo he de correr á palos' — and drew his sword. ⭐ Pío Pico (declaring himself 'vocal de la Diputación de este territorio') testifies he was at the fandango: Marrón challenged him '¿eres guapo ó eres mal criado?,' Pico drew and struck him, they grappled, Pico knocked him down with 'dos cintarazos,' then had Anastasio Machado return the cabo's sword. Other depositions (Javier Higuera, Sotelo, E. Higuera, Luis Morales) split between confirming and exculpating Carrillo. '(No se encuentra aquí más de esta sumaria.)' Orig. pp.504–528.

author: Ignacio del Valle, Ayudante de Plaza, Juez fiscal
themes: ecclesiastical-asylum; church-state; military-justice; san-diego; secularization-era; herrera; gómez; josé-sánchez; mexican-period
summary: The Ignacio Leonardo Herrera ecclesiastical-asylum causa (the concrete case behind Doc 93). The civilian Ignacio Leonardo Herrera (age 29, native of Guadalajara; escribano + 'principios de flebotomía') knifed the cavalry-sentinel Miguel Castro (cuts to arm/finger/back) on 17 May 1830, in revenge after Castro drove him 'á cintarazos' from the calabozo (where he'd gone to give prisoner Hilario García tobacco) and mocked him; Herrera pleaded he acted 'ciego de cólera.' He then fled the jail in his shackles and took refuge in the Mission San Diego church, claiming ecclesiastical immunity (asilo/retraimiento) — touching off a long church-vs-state battle. Fiscal Ignacio del Valle extracted him under a 'papel de iglesia' (caución juratoria) citing the order of 7 Oct 1775; Fr. Vicente Pasqual de Oliva (SD) and Father-President Fr. José Sánchez (San Gabriel) defended the asylum (Gregorian bull *Cum alias nonnulli*; Benedict XIII/XIV; the 1814 Francisco de Asís precedent), while Asesor Lic. [Rafael] Gómez ruled the crime excepted (alevosía; the bull 'no está recibida' in Spain; R. Órdenes 1750/1775/1787/1794). Outcome: Herrera sentenced to 8 años de presidio (Gómez, San Carlos 6 Nov; Echeandía decreed 22 Nov; finalized 19 Jan 1831); SD cmdt. Santiago Argüello protested Herrera was 'sentenciado sin oír el alegato de su defensor.' → verbatim in Expanded Entry B. ⚠️ This Herrera (civilian scribe, b. Guadalajara) is distinct from subcomisario José Mª Herrera (the Solís ally). Orig. pp.535–645.
cite: Dep. State Papers, Benicia (Military), MS, p. 535–645, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 19, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 93–116 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n93–n116)
