themes: pasquines; anti-echeandía; monterey; josé-castro; j-b-alvarado; californio-identity; political; mexican-period
summary: Causa 'sobre pasquines contra Echeandía.' Placards reading 'Muera Echandía' (sic) 'en letras grandes imitando la de imprenta' appeared at Monterey on 6–7 Dec 1830 in three spots — at Echeandía's house, on the bridge between Mariano Estrada's and Juan [Rogers] Cooper's houses, and at Esteban Munrás's house. Soldier Juan José Navarro (Mazatlán squadron) saw two muffled figures near Echeandía's door at ~2 AM, one seemingly José Castro 'el mozo'; Echeandía suspected Castro, motive 'odiosidad á los Mexicanos del Centro.' The fiscal swept up the young Californio elite: ⭐ José Castro deposed as 'secretario del Ilustre Ayuntamiento de Monterey,' and ⭐ Juan Bautista Alvarado as 'secretario de la Diputación del Territorio' (both said they were together at Castro's quarters that night; neither knew the author). Other witnesses: Joaquín Ortega, Joaquín Gómez, Joaquín de la Torre, José Amesti (Munrás's administrator), illiterate soldier Emeterio Espinosa. No author found — '(Aquí cesa el procedimiento.)' Escribano cabo Pedro Guerrero. An eve-of-1831 anti-Echeandía / Californio-vs-'Mexicanos del Centro' episode featuring the future 1836-movement leaders (Castro, Alvarado) as young men. ⚠️ scan n122 is a retake of printed p.121 (the scan index runs ahead of the printed page from n123 on). Orig. pp.759–782.

themes: solis-revolt; trial; sumaria; herrera; foreigners; hartnell; spence; stearns; missions; vaquero; ríos; solís; luis-antonio-martínez; vallejo; alvarado; josé-castro; monterey; 1829
summary: The Solís-revolt sumaria (declarations & confessions). Echeandía forwards declarations by Juan B. Alvarado, Ignacio Vallejo & José Castro, all naming J. Mª Herrera as the revolt's promoter / author of the Plan. Confessions of the accused (cabo Andrés de León, 21, owns his signature on the Plan but calls it Vaquero's work) narrate the night of the rising at Monterey: Solís named Mariano Vaquero sergeant/artillery commander; at 2 AM Vaquero woke the troops crying 'el enemigo está encima,' and the rebels (Vaquero, Raimundo de la Torre, Pablo Vejar, Prudencio & Lucas Espinosa, Juan Berbón[?], Leonardo Aceves, José Rosas…) arrested the officers — Alf. M. G. Vallejo, Subtte. Juan José Rocha, Comisario Manuel Jimeno Casarín, sargto Andrés Cervantes — and jailed them; they also seized J. B. Alvarado & José Castro (⚠️ so the young Californios were here *victims* of the rebels, though suspected of anti-Echeandía agitation a year later — Doc 96); a party rode to San Carlos for the Alcalde (not found). Vaquero planned a forced 10% commercial contribution (~$1,000) to buy arms and flee by ship. ⭐⭐⭐ Petronilo Ríos confessed he *wrote* the Plan from Herrera's *dictation* (15 Nov), read 'á Solís y á algunos extranjeros q[u]e allí estaban' before the troops. Joaquín Solís's own confession (16 Nov; age 37, b. Huejotzingo, Puebla; a convict deported for public works) deflects authorship to Herrera, claiming he was deceived into thinking the document was a petition to the Comandante General, not a Plan; he took $1,006 of municipal funds. ⭐⭐⭐ Named foreign-resident circle around Herrera (n173): 'los extranjeros q[u]e estaban con Herrera eran Guillermo (William) Hartnell, David Spence, Esteban (Stephen) Anderson, J. Mecala[?] (= McCulloch?), Abel Stearns y oficiales de buques balleneros.' The missions gave the rebels forced 'voluntary' contributions (San Luis Obispo, Purísima, Santa Inés; later Santa Cruz $100, San José $200, San Juan Bautista $40); friars José Sánchez (briefly named troop commander) and Vicente Sarría also figure (Sarría 'de indulto' at Monterey). ⚠️ Foreigners & missions repeatedly placed at the revolt's core (cf. the Plan's Art. 8 + the 'revolución por España' framing). ⭐ A later confession denies knowing whether Solís had any conversation with Fr. Martínez 'sobre el pronunciamiento por España' (the friar-conspiracy probe). ⚠️ Petronilo Ríos's story evolved — his Nov-1829 declaration (he *wrote* the Plan from Herrera's dictation) softened by Apr 1830 to merely signing it 'porque se le obligó' (the draft in Vaquero's hand). The rank-and-file confessions (Espinosa, Rosas, Aces…) uniformly disclaim involvement and agree the revolt's origin was unpaid wages. Solís's formal confession before the consejo de guerra (21 Apr 1830, defender Tte. Manuel Ibarra) re-narrates the rising, names foreign merchant Juan (John) Cooper & '[Simón] Bautista' as witnesses, and claims he protected Alf. Vallejo when Arenas wanted to kill him 'como un perro'; Solís surrendered under the April indulto to Alf. Francisco Pacheco. The remaining defendant confessions (Prudencio Espinosa, Pablo Vejar, Melitón Soto [the revolt's courier of the Plan to the ayuntamientos & diputados for $30], Máximo Guerra [a Chilean artilleryman, 31]…) repeat the arrests + unpaid-wages motive; a lista de presos names the 14 (Solís, R. de la Torre, Máximo Guerra, Melitón Soto, Vaquero, Antonio Guevara, Vejar, Ignacio Lara, Serapio Escamilla, Victorino & Gonzalo Altamirano, Leonardo Aces, Inés Solano, Gabriel de la Torre). ⭐⭐⭐ The counter-revolution (n195): the Alcalde led armed foreigners gathered at John Cooper's house + Juan B. Alvarado + vecinos to retake the Monterey artillery barracks and arrest Vaquero & Cervantes — the foreign community as *armed suppressors* of the revolt (complicating the 'extranjeros con Herrera' picture). ⭐ Herrera's plot is said to have counted on Capt. Miguel González, a surgeon (Cobata[?]), and Diputado Vicente Sánchez (cf. Docs 143–144). ⚠️ retake scans n187 (p.183) & n193 (p.188); printed page = scan − 5 from n194. ⭐⭐⭐ David Spence's deposition (comerciante, 23 June 1830) is the one clearly-deposed foreigner: Herrera summoned him, another ship captain & Stephen Anderson to his house, read them the Plan & asked their opinion (some answered 'está bueno' out of courtesy; Solís present as signer) — concrete *documented* foreign involvement. ⚠️ The Hartnell/Anderson/Stearns/McCulloch circle was *named* in Solís's confession (n173), but only Spence's own deposition appears here (don't over-claim the others deposed). The proceso also appends Solís's actual revolt-period orders as evidence (n208) — incl. the 28 Nov salute order to Cabo Joaquín Piña (Mis.n Dolores): three artillery discharges (on entry, on the Plan's approval, on the troops' retirement) — the primary document behind Expanded Entry A. A deposition at n204 also explains Art. 8's pro-Spanish addition was inserted at the request of Spaniards fearing the proceedings. ⚠️ Scans n197–n208 gap-sampled (key findings captured, not every leaf transcribed — completeness pass pending). The 'revolución por España' autos follow (Doc 149). Orig. pp.162–203+.

author: Echeandía / Zamorano (fiscal)
themes: solis-revolt; revolución-por-españa; fernando-vii; luis-antonio-martínez; missionary; expulsion; anderson; anti-spanish; máximo-guerra; santa-inés; monterey; 1830
summary: The 'revolución por España' autos — the prosecution of Fr. Luis Antonio Martínez. Echeandía orders the inquiry; the file's cover sheet (carátula) reads 'Autos q[u]e aclaran q[u]e el objeto de la facción de Solís, era el de pronunciarse en favor del Gob.no Español.' Testimony implicates the San Luis Obispo missionary Fr. Luis Antonio Martínez: Lázaro Piña (23 Jan) saw artilleryman Máximo Guerra (a Chilean) in league with Fr. Martínez at Santa Inés, who advised 'pronunciarse por España'; a paper read 'Viva Fernando 7º' (with 3 initials); the Padre promised to recommend them to 'su amo Fernandito' (Ferdinand VII). Francisco Becerra (San Blas inf.): the friar [or Sarría?] at SLO offered Guerra money & goods to pronounce for Spain. Calls to prosecute Fr. Martínez, Máximo Guerra, R. de la Torre, Melitón Soto. ⭐⭐ Fr. Martínez allegedly had ~$6,000 embarked on the schooner *La Paloma* to flee to Spain (per Capt. Miguel González, n222); the planned cry 'dar el grito por España' at SLO with 14 vaqueros per mission. ⭐⭐⭐ Fr. Martínez's own defense (n228): he denies the pro-Spanish charge, claiming he was an *early supporter of independence* ('quizás fui yo el primero de mis hermanos… q[u]e dije, tal debe seguir la suerte de la república; así opinaba y así opino ahora'), requests his passport to leave the Republic, protests the violation of civil & canon law, and cites his gota (gout). The asesor's deliberation (n234): given his age/ailments and the fear that the other missionaries would abandon the missions if a 'persona consagrada' were jailed, he is not imprisoned but expelled — the record finding he 'auxilió á la facción de Solís p[ar]a el pronunciamiento en favor de la España.' ⭐⭐⭐ The verdict (n235–n236): a war-council of officers voted 5 to 1 — citing the territory's 'tranquilidad y seguridad' and Martínez's 'inculpabilidad' (i.e., *not* a guilty finding) plus his 26 Dec 1826 declaration that he did not conform with 'nuestro actual sistema' (the republic) — to compel his expulsion on any non-Spanish ship (with a bond to carry him to Europe or the US). Frs. Pedro & Juan Cabot filed manifestos in his favor; fiscal Tte. de Ing. Miguel García Lobato. Fr. Martínez was put aboard the foreign merchant Stephen Anderson's English frigate 'Thomas Nowlan' (7 Mar 1832), swearing not to disembark at Manila or the Sandwich Islands [Hawaii] but to take the first ship to Europe. (⚠️ Anderson, named in the Solís depositions, owned the *deportation* ship — the foreign community central yet again.) This closes the Solís dossier and Tomo LXXII ('Fin del tomo 72,' n236). ⚠️ n209–n234 gap-sampled (completeness pass pending for verbatim depositions). Orig. pp.204–231 (stamp '659' = 359).

summary: Causa criminal vs. José Mariano Duarte, Alcalde of San José, for getting the ayuntamiento to sign 'subversive' papers. Denounced by síndico Luis Chabolla[?]; the drafts (in the archive, extracted by Regidor Flores) deemed 'subversivos y de mucha malicia.' Doc nº1 (in the Alcalde's own hand): a federalist manifesto — 'este Ayuntam.to ha llegado á conocer sus derechos y el alcance de sus fuerzas' — calling (per constitutional art. 27) for the Exma Diputación to be convened at Monterey at the ayuntamientos' petition. Doc nº2: accusations the alcalde was caught in 'tratos ilícitos' with Ignacia Padilla at night (regidores Joaquín Higuera + Fernando Félix expelling him). ⚠️ The political agitation echoes the Solís Plan's central demand (reconvene the Diputación) and is an apparent precursor to the Nov-1831 anti-Victoria revolt. Docs nº3–4: the acta (1 June 1831) expanding the San José ayuntamiento — adding 2 regidores (Fernando Félix & Cnt. Rodríguez), secretary José Reyes Berreyesa, depositario the retired sgt Luis Peralta (the prominent ranchero). Witness Luis Chabolla (síndico): Duarte's circular invited the Territory's ayuntamientos to press the Cmdt. Gen. to convene the Diputación Provincial ('redunda en la felicidad del país'); Chabolla demurred (the matter belonged to the Diputación itself). Also alleged arbitrary acts (jailing a woman & asking Santa Clara's padre to shackle/shear her — the padre refused) + a municipal-funds dispute. Escribano Petronilo Ríos. Secretary José Reyes Berreyesa refused to copy/sign paper nº1, warning it meant attacking the Jefe Superior (Gov. Victoria); the Alcalde nonetheless sent the copy to Antonino Buelna (alcalde at Monterey — a 1831-revolt figure). Witness Mª Ignacia Padilla (true name Mª Presentación Lóngora[?]) detailed the alcalde's mistreatment (shackling her in jail). ⭐⭐⭐ Duarte's confession (n264–66): the plan originated at Monterey on 7 Apr 1831 in conversation with Antonino Buelna (Monterey alcalde), the Secretary of the Provincial Diputación [= J. B. Alvarado], and José Castro — to petition the Cmdt. Gen. to convene the Diputación; Buelna later came to San José, and Duarte signed the document Buelna forwarded to Monterey. (So the San José case ties directly into the Buelna / Castro / Alvarado federalist circle behind the Nov-1831 anti-Victoria revolt — the same young Californios as the Solís pasquines, Doc 96.) Fiscal Pliego: Duarte guilty by his own confession + the witnesses; the case moved to Monterey to depose the implicated Antonino Buelna (19 Aug), who denied remembering the Diputación plan. Defender Tte. Juan Mª Ibarra. José Castro (Monterey ayuntamiento secretary) & J. B. Alvarado (Diputación secretary) both deposed — distancing themselves from a direct alcalde-to-alcalde conspiracy while confirming the Monterey ayuntamiento DID form actas to convene the Diputación. ⭐⭐ Gov. Victoria's framing (24 Aug oficio): the agitation was 'procurar por medios ilegales se reuniese la Diputación, con fines siniestros y muy contrarios á las determinaciones del Sup.o Gob.,' with Buelna the key inducer — the government casting the federalist movement as subversion (the tension that exploded into the Nov-1831 revolt). The fiscal's summary (n280–85) restates the 3 charges: (1) pressing the ayuntamientos to convene the Diputación (a paper in Duarte's own hand, f.2); (2) his 7 Jul suspension over the night-time illicit-relations incident (f.3); (3) the arbitrary 1 June election of 2 regidores + secretary + depositario (f.5). ⚠️ n275–n285 gap-sampled (witness ratifications/careos + the summary; payload captured — completeness pass could fill these leaves). ⭐⭐ Conclusion (n286–88): the Asesor ruled the military lacked jurisdiction over alcaldes acting as first-instance judges, so the case was remitted to the Mexican Supreme Court (ministers Flores/Navarrete/Guzmán, Feb–Mar 1832) for civil handling + a Jefe-Político report on the alcaldes' 'crime' of trying to convene the Diputación. ⚠️ By then Victoria had already been overthrown — the prosecution was moot.

themes: fiscal-corruption; malversation; herrera; solis-revolt-backstory; nile; tepic; intendant-ordinance; zamorano; bandini; monterey; 1827
summary: Secret causa vs. subcomisario José Mª Herrera for malversación de caudales públicos. Echeandía commissioned Zamorano (25 Apr 1827, SB) to secretly investigate Herrera's 'dispersión' of public funds during his management. Witness Capt. José de la Guerra: Herrera received $22,000 cash for 7 months' troop pay, but only ~$3,600/month reached the SB company — implying diversion. (The pre-Solís backstory: Herrera under embezzlement investigation in 1827, before becoming the 1829 revolt's financial mastermind — cf. the Plan's grievance over his suspension.) Filed out of order in this 1831 tomo. Witnesses (de la Guerra, Maitorena, Carlos Antonio Carrillo, Juan Bandini, Romualdo Pacheco) establish the $22,000 was shipped from Acapulco on the berg. *Morelos* then via San Blas on the goleta *Nieves* (toward Loreto); the shortfall traced to Herrera spending part on goods (cigars, effects) at Tepic; only ~$3,600/mo reached the SB company. Also names a customs/otter-duty waiver Herrera granted the American brig *Nile* (Oct 1825). Merchant Luis Bringas (the goods' seller) deposed at LA: the goods (~$45,000 worth) came from Tepic (financed by Saltillo merchant Salvador Tejada + a Herrera relative, guarantor Ramón Pareja); Herrera helped ship them on the warship *Morelos*, and they were sold from Herrera's own house then peddled at the presidios/pueblos/missions — the heart of the malversation question (public office aiding a private import venture). Courier Ignacio Mª Alvarado (paid $30 by Bringas to carry letters to Herrera) deposed; financial detail names a draft to the American merchant Guillermo (William A.) Gale. ⭐ Conclusion (n312, fiscal Capt. summary: 'Sedición de Antonio Ávila' — investigation of a convict-band uprising in the 1832 civil conflict. Antonio Ávila led a band of presidiarios (from Santa Margarita) recruited & armed by Don Vicente Sánchez (the LA diputado; arms taken from Santa Bárbara, distributed at the Cerrito de los Voluntarios). The plan: join the Mazatlán squadron under Tte. Ibarra to fight the 'San Diego party' / oppose Zamorano (the northern Comandante), framed 'en defensa del Supremo Gob.no'; comisario Joaquín Gómez (SB) supplied goods; documents from Mariano Estrada, Rafael Gómez, Joaquín Gómez named. Six convict-deserters (Ignacio Olgadillo, Antonio Rivera, José Mª Blanquel, Catarino López, Joaquín Alfaro, Guadalupe Martínez) deposed — they deserted on realizing they'd been deceived by Sánchez & Ávila. A key datapoint on the 1832 post-Victoria civil war (Zamorano's north vs. Echeandía/Sánchez's south). ⭐⭐ Vicente Sánchez claimed parliamentary immunity (as a territorial Diputado, Const. Art. 336 + the 24 May 1813 Cortes decree) to refuse testifying; Asesor Gómez ruled the immunity didn't cover an act 'muy distante de sus atribuciones.' ⭐⭐ Conclusion: Gov. Figueroa (1833) dismissed the whole case under the AMNESTY law of 25 April 1832 — the accused already free & the cause unsubstantiated; sobreseído y archivado. ⚠️ n355–n362 gap-sampled (repetitive convict-deserter testimony).

summary: Sentence in the San Diego Indian-uprising conspiracy. Investigated by Argüello, continued by fiscal Nicolás Gutiérrez under Figueroa/Gómez → consejo de guerra (pres. Capt. Juan Antonio Muñoz; vocales Zamorano, González, Navarrete, Peña; Alf. Francisco Pacheco). summary: The fullest account of the 1832 civil war. Ávila's 2nd petition: he headed a band of presidiarios 'para restablecer la autoridad legítima contra los que se levantaron en San Diego y destruyeron al… Cap. Político D. Manuel Victoria,' asking return of the arms confiscated in 1832 + a passport to return to Mexico by land. Zamorano's informe: the arms were seized not for the anti-Victoria action but later, 'por haberse puesto á la cabeza de una partida de presidiarios que alarmó de acuerdo con D. Vicente Sánchez, vecino… de los Ángeles, para destituirme'; narrates the pursuit (Alf. Anastasio Carrillo, 25 men), the split with Sánchez ~8 leagues past Mission San Buenaventura (Sánchez meant to attack San Diego, counting on Tte. Ibarra's division), the presidiarios abandoning Ávila 'por verse engañados' and surrendering at Mission Santa Inés. author: witnesses/accused; decree by Nicolás Gutiérrez
summary: (cont.) San Luis Rey / Temecula conspiracy. Julián urged all to oppose giving the 'Rancho de Temécula á S.E. [José Antonio] Estudillo,' since the ex-mission had no dominion in those lands; the Genl had taken much ex-mission cattle unpaid → lands 'ya estaba perdida'; plot to distribute lands & kill all; correos Julián & Andrés sent to summon the gentiles; ref. the earlier conspiracy under Gov. Victoria. Witnesses: 2nd Marcial, 3rd Alejo, 4th José Marcial, 5th Andrés; declaraciones preparatorias of Juan Nepomuceno, José Miguel & Julián Murillo (named as ringleader). Fiscal interrogated 17 Apr. Gutiérrez decree, Monterey 5 Nov 1835: 'Habiendo noticia que los acusados se hallan en libertad por disposición del Sor Comandte Genl mi antecesor, archívese esta sumaria = Gutiérrez' (pp.380–414).

summary: The volume's tail — a heavily *interleaved* run of fiscal/postal/muster records across many years (NOT chronological): ⭐⭐ Nicolás Gutiérrez's private 1836 letter to Gov. The only Russian/HBC trace is HBC agent Rae's port-dues (n380/n382). Not in this Military series.

summary: MARQUEE, copied VERBATIM: 'Señor mío: esta mañana he recibido las dos cartas que V.S. se dignó de escribirme después de la llegada á ese puerto de S. Francisco á donde arribó… con su embarcación precisado de los fuertes temporales que ha sufrido en el último equinoccio. Me alegro mucho… y de ofrecer con franqueza á la disposición con V.S. y de la Expedición Rusa á quien tengo órden de mi Soberano de facilitarle los auxilios… le suplico á V.S. se sirva pasarme una relación ó nota de lo que necesite para mandar yo inmediatamente se le socorra tanto á V.S. como para su tripulación… debo expresar que viva V.S. entendido de que no tendrá motivo de variar de concepto… antes bien se ratificará en el interés que se toma la Nación Española en conservar toda armonía y atención con la Nación Rusa y en particular con la persona de V.S. = Por lo que y para realizar mis deseos de conocer á V.S., ofrecerme de cerca y evitarle la caminata que se le ofrecería por tierra para venir á Monterrey estoy dispuesto el pasar á verle á V.S. la semana entrante.'

summary: MARQUEE — 'Instrucciones pa gobernar': lo nombra Juez del Rl de Sta Anna y poblaciones y Misiones inmediatas. Arts. 1–21: 1ª buena conducta 'ó, al menos, aparentarla'; 2ª justicia con imparcialidad, armonía en el vecindario, 'suave y moderado con los delincuentes'; 3ª se impondrá de las órdenes archivadas; 4ª remediar abusos; 5ª maduro exámen á las quejas; 6ª los abusos mas notables del distrito: 'las enemistades continuas producidas por el odio, los intereses, la embriaguez y amancebamiento' — castigo con cepo; 7º–8º vigilar ociosos y vagabundos; 9º informará sobre la conducta de las mugeres casadas en ausencia de sus maridos y de las viudas y solteras que viven solas (amonestación reservada 1ª y 2ª vez); 10º jugadores en cuadrillas; 11º justicia á pobres y ricos con rectitud… sin correr traslado á otro funcionario para evitar demoras; 12º diligencias como cabeza de proceso; 13º ganado alzado ú orejano → infractores á Loreto; 14º arancel sobre venta de frutos del país; 15º bando de Gálvez: azogue al precio de la Administración de Álamos; 16º Ramo de Tabaco bajo el Administrador J. Mª Estrada; 17º Alcabalas, Sal, Diezmos y Ganado Orejano á su cuidado; 18º informe de los dueños de posesiones que adeuden á la Corona por las concesiones de terrenos; 20º armas prohibidas; 21º pasageros de las canoas: la 'gente paseante ú ociosa' devuelta en las mismas canoas. Instrucciones adicionales 1ª–11ª: 1ª quiebra del Habilitado Sargento L. López ya difunto; 2ª prohibición de fiar á los vecinos los productos de Rl Hacienda; 3ª demandas de salarios adelantados limitadas al bando de Gálvez sobre salarios (2–3 meses); 4ª deudas de particulares; 5ª bienes del finado José Castro; 6ª envío de plata de la hacienda de Ocio; 7ª en la ex-Misión de Santiago podrán establecerse otros vecinos reconociendo como cabeza principal á Salvador de Castro; 8ª de cuatro toros que se cojan, una vaca á cada vecino; 'solo á los indios está permitido coger ganado alzado para su gasto en el interior de la Misión, y el restante pertenece al Rey'; 9º el Cura: dos reses al mes; 10º vagos y ociosos; 11º Ramos de Real Hacda á cargo de Andrés Cota desde Marzo

author: Arrillaga/Solá
summary: 'Sobre encuentro y campaña con gentiles' — Arrillaga reports he ordered Alférez Gabriel Moraga of the SF company to pursue the gentiles of the 'ranchería llamada Sespesuya' north of the presidio, who in three years of nominal peace had killed 16 cristianos; the ranchería lay across the estero de S.n Francisco and the troops had no launches ('las tropas no tienen lanchas'), crossing by relays in one small boat found on the shore; Moraga took 18 gentile prisoners, released 'por estar muy mal heridos' and expected to die; survivors made a tenacious stand in three yacales, wounding 2 cabos and 2 soldiers (the troop's only casualties); after the occupants of two yacales were killed the cristianos fired the third to force surrender, 'pero no lo consiguieron; pues los valientes indios murieron envueltos en las llamas antes q.e entregarse'; the alférez could not count the dead ('no les contó por… darle compasión el destrozo') and reckoned ~120 gentiles in the fight. Arrillaga commends the troop, asking the grade of teniente for Moraga, sergeant for the wounded cabos, and an escudo de ventajas for the soldiers. [= the action of 22 May 1810; the royal reward order returned via the viceroy, Nov 1811 — see Prov. St. Pap. XIX]
cite: Provincial Records, MS, p. IX:367–71, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 25, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 371–372 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n374–n375)

summary: On encounters with the Indians — a rich borderlands + Indian-affairs dossier: Ewing Young ('Joaquín Young') and his 22-man party arrive at Mission San José (from the Valle de San Luis, a day from New Mexico), to buy horses & trap beaver; shows two English passports differing only in date (1828 & 1829) [= Clay passports, docs 250/288] + one sealed at the Mexican Legation, Washington, 20 Mar 1828; Young's Americans join Mission San José's Indian alcalde Francisco Ximénez, who raised a 450-man gentile-auxiliary army (Cosumnes/Ochejamenes etc.) to recover fugitive neophytes; the fugitive captain Huyumecsepa refuses to return them, saying at the mission 'solo les daban muchos azotes' (⭐ an Indian indictment of mission floggings); a 3-hour firefight; ⭐⭐⭐ intelligence that Estanislao, pardoned cabecilla of the prior year's (1829) neophyte revolt, is out in the Tulares with 100 horses under a padre's license, and on the San Joaquín rancherías' horse herds (Moquelumnes, the 'capitán general' Tinay)

summary: «Estado de la Iglesia en Cal.» — larga y angustiada jeremiada sobre el colapso del sistema misional tras la secularización (5 leaves). Recibió la nota que lo excita á poner en su Diócesis el Arancel de Párrocos, tan necesario desde que se quitó el sistema de Misiones que sostenía tanto á los Ministros como al culto. «V.E. y todos los Californios son testigos oculares de que estos 2 objetos se llenaron perfectamente desde la fundación de estos lugares hasta que se arruinaron»; los Misioneros nunca gravaron á los fieles con contribución alguna. ⭐ «4 años escasos hace que gobierno á esta nueva Iglesia y en este tpᵒ ¡oh! cuánto ha sufrido mi corazón!!»; S. Solano, S. Rafael, S. Francⁿ, S. Antⁿ, S. Juan Capistrano &c están sin sacerdotes; los indios «desgraciados que por la ruina de las Misiones han dejado doctrina, misas, sacramentos… unidos con los gentiles, viven ya como ellos, ó en un estado peor, y desmoralizados se han entregado al robo, á la embriaguez, á los asesinatos y á toda disolución»; no le ofrecieron hospedaje ni en S. Francⁿ ni en S. Solano. «Sin fondos, sin diezmos (porque muchos no quieren pagarlos), sin sacerdotes… sin escuelas… es imposible que progrese, y va caminando á su destrucción.» ⭐ El arancel no remediará los males. ⭐⭐ Estadística sacramental de Sta Bárbara (año ppᵒ): 55 bautismos, 4 matrimonios, 26 entierros; con el benignísimo Arancel del Obispado de Guadalajara (18 rs/bautismo, 7 pesos/matrimonio corriente, $6½/entierro humilde) la población solo pudo producir $326·6 rs de dros parroquiales al año «si se hubieran cobrado» — insuficiente para sostener un párroco; se irán despidiendo los PP uno tras otro y el Obispo dará cuenta á Su Santidad y al público «por medio de un manifiesto». No obstante, «como al enfermo deshauciado se le aplican todos los remedios», aceptará el remedio del arancel si el vecindario lo pide oficialmente (Monterey, S. José, Sta Bárbara &c). Incluye la carta del R.P. Mtro de Monterey [Suárez del Real]
cite: Departmental State Papers, MS, tom. VI, p. 491–494, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 30, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 266–271 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n268–n273)

summary: VERBATIM installation acta + Figueroa's long installation DISCOURSE (1 May 1834) — 'una era nueva se dibuja… la aurora de la libertad… California, este pueblo naciente arrancado de las cadenas en que yacía bajo la dura servidumbre de los descendientes de Cortés se eleva… bajo el sistema federativo.' summary: ✓ FULLY VERIFIED vs scans n19–n22 (2026-07-06): date/parties, the '9 Nov 1824' Monterey contract, $14,000 round-trip freight, the $10,000 'libre de cámara' clause, and — verbatim on n20 — 'las 375 pieles de nutria en Canton… á $18¾ una con otra' all confirmed. *(This $18¾ Canton resale is the figure cross-referenced for the [[ca3-prov-state-papers-v-vi-survey]] Doc 445 otter-tariff correction — now independently verified.)* The Cooper/*Rover* otter-contract accounting. Arbitration of the pending accounts from the contract Gov. Luis A. Argüello made (auth. by the Diputación) with Capt. John R. Cooper to send the schr *Rover* to Canton with government otter skins. Panel: Cooper, Juan Bandini (govt), Wm A. Richardson (interpreter/price-expert), w/ Cristóbal Palomares & José A. Carrillo (diputados). 375 skins sold in Canton @ $18¾ each; effects delivered to Domingo Carrillo (habilitado, San Diego). Full contract (Monterey, 9 Nov 1824): Cooper to fit *Rover* for an Asia voyage sailing early Jan 1825; province pays $14,000 round-trip freight; $10,000 duty-free ('libre de cámara'); vessel not to leave Canton overloaded. Echeandía declares the Canton sale/costs 'no plenamente justificada' but leaves liability on Cooper for the Supreme Govt to judge.

Descripción de la Bahía de San Francisco y sus recursos.' A fiscal-military-commercial treatise arguing to (1) absolutely prohibit foreign ships from the *comercio de escala y cabotaje* (citing the law of 16 Nov 1827, art. 5 cap. 1: '*Los buques estrangeros no podrán hacer el comercio de escala, ni el de cabotaje en los puertos de la república*'); (2) transfer the Aduana Marítima from Monterey to San Francisco (recalling the 1829 order that let the *gefe político* choose the port + the 1829 move to San Diego); vivid on the contraband economy — ships tolerated to touch Sta Bárbara/SF 'antes y despues de su aforo,' ballast-trick declarations ('cajas de tabaco vacías, petates de Sandwich, escobas, millares de cohetitos de china'), reloading contraband from 'lugares poco frecuentados.' Then a detailed description of San Francisco Bay: the Golden Gate ('dos grandes cabos que distan… mas de una milla,' puntas de los Reyes y Lobos), Angel I. ('la de los Ángeles… la llave de todo el [golfo]') + Fort Point castillo ('por naturaleza una fortaleza invencible'); the three rivers Sacramento, San Joaquín y Jesús María navigable >100 leguas; the 'mar de Sta Clara' (South Bay); abundant shipbuilding timber; climate 'mas benigna que la de Monterey'; the settlements S. Francisco, Dolores, Alvarado (San José Guadalupe), ex-misión de San José, Sta Clara, Sonoma, San Rafael + 17 haciendas (Buriburi, S. Antonio, El Pinole, S. Pablo, Sta Teresa, Pulgas…) + >25 ranchos owning 'mas de ciento cincuenta mil reses.' Individuals include: Antonio Sunol (vecino de S. summary: 'Informe general sobre California' — a comprehensive sectioned state-of-the-territory economic survey (Expanded-Entry candidate): *Agricultura* (wheat/grains, vineyards as the future export; ⭐ the indigenous natives 'han sido siempre y son hasta la fecha los únicos brazos laboriosos del país'); *Crías* (cattle/sheep/wild 'mesteña' horses); *Manufacturas* (mission-neophyte textiles/crafts; cattle hides the only export; 'falta de brazos'); ⭐⭐⭐ *Pesca* (otter & beaver 'could have been the principal element' but foreigners exploit them fraudulently, buying pelts cheap from the natives; no national ship to stop them destroying the island otter-grounds; SF-Bay-river beaver the great untapped resource); *Minas* (no valuable minerals known, iron most common — pre-Gold-Rush); ⭐⭐ *Epidemias* (smallpox rare so vaccination neglected, no physician in the whole territory, venereal disease 'devouring' the neophytes, mission medicine-chests 'no sirven de nada'; the mission regime 'no proporcionado á la salud de los indígenas,' their condition 'muy lastimosa, digna de lamentarse' — a governor's mission-health indictment); *Población* / *Milicia local* / *Tranquilidad pública* (the 1829 Solís revolution) / *Seguridad* (the vast fertile country's wealth 'excita la codicia,' keep criminal colonists out). Complete: scan n132–n139, tomo pp. 336–346

summary: Informe of his *visita* to the Southern (Baja California) department: visited missions San José del Cabo, Santiago, Todos Santos, Real de Sta Ana etc.; sale of *azogue* (mercury) at the presidio *habilitación* aided the miners; *reales de minas* so destitute nobody risks goods, all on credit (only $1,250 traded in 1784); ordered ranchers to register brands (*fierros y marcas*, $6/título) & show land titles; Viceroy Gálvez ruled mission lands only provisional; ceded 2 sitios at Todos Santos to Crisóstomo Castro; Todos Santos mission debt $2,081 paid 1784; '4 yrs since a grain of maize grew'; urged an Indian *Gobernador* so neophytes get justice ('los jueces del departamento no hacían caso de los indios'); mission cattle to supply the 3 *reales de minas* at $3/toro (disputed)

New Mexico & Texas 'bastante temible'); (f) rebuts the federal charge (Doc 27) that he usurped the Indians' faculty — his bando's Art. 2 had the ayuntamiento name the administrators; acted w/ the Diputación's consent, 'in favor of los reducidos'; (g) ⭐⭐⭐ 'los bienes de las misiones son de los reducidos en ellas' (mission property belongs to the neophytes — the ground for distributing it to them; invokes Neve's 1781 Reglamento); (h) a 2nd population figure — ~13,000 reducidos ≈ ⅘ of the Territory (vs the 8,000 'forzados'); aim to 'arruinar de una vez el poder de los Misioneros'; ties in Herrera's fiscal abuse + friar-royalism/Solís revolt (ends n57 — a ~35-page apologia, tomo pp.131–166)

themes: secularization; duran; figueroa; gradualist; bishopric; clero-patricio; neophyte-property; diezmos; echeandia-bando; californio
summary: Durán's *Manifiesto/Informe* on the secularization of the missions — his reply to Figueroa's 29 Aug 1833 charge to report which missions qualify under the 13 Sept 1813 law, in two points. (1) All Alta-California missions except San Francisco Solano exceed the 10-year rule (most by 20–30 yrs) → by the letter all could be secularized, but the 10-yr rule was set 'sin conocimientos topográficos… relativos á este País.' (2) The *inconvenientes y peligros* → urges GRADUAL secularization: the neophytes lack the 'disposición' for premature property-ownership (made owners they would sell/abandon and flee 'á los montes y tulares á vivir de la naturaleza'); soldiers unpaid 23 yrs; frontier danger of gentiles arming via foreigners; the neophyte-property/*diezmos* question. ⭐⭐ concedes Echeandía's 6 Jan 1831 bando 'practicado de buena fe… sin comparación mucho más ventajosa que el sistema actual' — yet as a Fernandino 'protesto contra ella.' ⭐⭐⭐ his ecclesiastical alternative — found a *bishopric*, train a native 'clero patricio' from 'hijos de familia decentes y honradas,' a *seminario* + Colegio de Misioneros funded by *diezmos* — THEN a general secularization could proceed safely 'sin el riesgo de dispersarse estas Cristiandades.' Grounds his authority in '27 años… de servir estas misiones'; ✒ 'Yo siempre pecaré más por retenerme que por progresista.' ✅ FLAG RESOLVED 2026-07-09 (leaf re-read n83–95): a single, distinct Durán document — NOT a re-copy of Echeandía's Doc 32 (the pro-bando lines are Durán's third-person concession, not Echeandía's first-person apologia). The gradualist / ecclesiastical pole of the 1833 debate — complements García Diego's *parecer* (Doc 38) & Figueroa's report (Doc 37); ⚠ header date read as '3' of a month (transmittal Doc 41 = 3 Oct) — treat as Sept–Oct 1833, re-transcribe the exact date before citing. → [[californio-article]] secularization spine
cite: State Papers, Missions and Colonization, MS, tom. II, p. 84–96 (doc's own pp. 201–6), Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 53, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 84–96 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n83–95)

summary: 'Informe RESERVADO sobre el Establecimiento de Ross' — Vallejo's first-person military reconnaissance of the Russian coast/interior (EXPANDED-ENTRY CANDIDATE). Part 1 (n97–104): left Ross the 28th, reached Puerto de Bodega (7 leguas off) = 4 wooden factory-buildings the Russians built to serve their ships/foreigners and export what they extract; the Bodega + 'San Francisco alias Los Tamales' bay geography (navigable, small craft 6 leguas inland); ⭐⭐⭐ at Bodega permanently only 'una Capitanía de gentiles' — 43 people under Captain *Guchactac* — whose purpose is to GUARD the Russian factories (unmolested by other Indians; San Rafael mission-Indian scouts, 'un tal Rafael'); ⭐⭐ Indian grievances/intelligence (soldiers luring gentiles & fugitive Christians then imprisoning them → San Rafael/Sonoma to Christianize; Indians 'resueltos á morir' — ⚠ rough paleography, transcribe before quoting); rode inland to Santa Rosa (12 leguas from Bodega) — the arroyo where the Russians farmed 'dos años hace' (~1831), depopulated rancherías (Selayomi), irrigable lands, ⭐ 'abunda de castores' (beaver/otter) + 'vestigios de los antiguos pescadores'; ⭐⭐⭐ Santa Rosa/Jaquiximi has 'las mejores circunstancias para la fundación de un pueblo' (the reconnaissance behind the Sonoma-frontier counter-colonization); his Indian-pacification diplomacy; ⭐⭐⭐ a denunciation of the missionaries' 'mala fé, maltrato y crueldad… sistema sanguinario… ¡Qué monstruosidades!' as the root of frontier-Indian hostility. Part 2 (n105–n111, ✅ BOUNDARY RESOLVED 2026-07-11 on a leaf re-read — it IS continuous first-person Vallejo, NOT a spliced re-copy: n104's mission-cruelty denunciation flows directly into 'todos los medios que estuvieron á mi alcance… según V.S. me encargó… por conducto del Comandante [Barón] Wrangel'): strategic intelligence on the wider Russian establishment — the RAC Pacific network (Ross, Unalaska, Kodiak, Kamchatka), Ross ~400 people + fortifications against native uprisings + a fleet (13 vessels: 3 frigates, 9 brigs) + peltry commerce + Ross livestock (~800 cattle, 100 horses, 200 sheep, 60 pigs), citing data via Wrangel/'el Comandante.' Part 3 — the Ross-fort reconnaissance (n107–110, the fuller extent the earlier gap-sample missed): the orchard of 400 fruit trees, 2 mills (one wind, one water), and the buildings/ships for the peltry trade; the fort itself — ~300 people; a wooden quadrilateral stockade with 12 artillery pieces on 2 corner bastions/blockhouses + 6 more inside a loopholed building + 3 at the Comandante's house (marine carriages); '39 edificios,' 4 inside the walls; the governor of Sitka expected at Ross ~12 June 1833; and the Ross Comandante's offer of 36 men to help attack the hostile Indians, which Vallejo declined ('aunque el objeto no era hostil'). ⚠ the '39 edificios / 4 dentro de la muralla' description in n107–110 partly REPEATS an earlier building count — possible internal re-copy/overlap in this re-copy-heavy volume; verify verbatim before quoting the fort structure. Closes n111 with the patriotic peroration — cooperate 'al esplendor… de mi Nación y á la prosperidad de esta parte preciosa é interesante de la Gran República Mejicana.' → [[russian-california]] KEYSTONE, [[bodega-primary-sources]], [[project_solano_county_future]] (Santa Rosa/Bodega/Guchactac), [[indian-raiding-article]] (mission-cruelty denunciation + Indian labor for the Russians). ✅ document extent now FIXED = n97–n111 (Doc 46 begins mid-n111). ⚠ full verbatim TX still pending — all figures/quotes are scale-2 abstracts to verify at scale 4 before citing.

themes: secularization; missions; land-tenure; solares; semovientes; anti-alienation; emancipados; pueblo; figueroa; zamorano; californio; indian
summary: 'Reglamento Provisional para la secularización de las Misiones de la Alta California' (*Doc. impreso*) — the foundational secularization decree: per the spirit of the 17 Aug 1833 law & the Supremo Gobierno's instructions, the missions partially converted to pueblos beginning Aug (10 first, then the rest); the padres relieved of temporalities & confined to spiritual ministry until formal parish division; territorial govt reassumes temporalities. Distribución de intereses y terrenos: each family head & everyone over 20 (even without family) gets from the missions' common lands a solar ≤ 400 varas + watering commons, with ejidos & propios per pueblo; half the livestock (*semovientes*) & up to half the tools distributed proportionally; the surplus held under a Gefe-Político-named administrator (approved by the Sup. Gob. Federal); provision for padres' subsistence, mayordomo pay, worship, schools & police from the common mass. Gobierno Político de los Pueblos: ayuntamientos formed, elections held; economic govt to the ayuntamientos, contentious justice to the nearest 1ª-instancia judges; emancipados owe communal labor on the still-undivided vineyards/orchards & personal service to the padre. Prevenciones — Art. 18 anti-alienation: emancipated Indians may not sell, encumber or alienate granted lands or cattle; violating sales are void, the govt reclaims, buyers lose their money; heirless lands revert to the emancipated body (art. 19). Art. 22 bars padres from large-scale cattle slaughter before enactment; passive mission debts preferred (art. 23)

summary: THE Híjar Instructions — 'Instrucciones á que deberá arreglar su conducta D.n José Mª de Híjar, Gefe Político de la Alta California y Director de la Colonización de esta y de la Baja.' Art. 1: 'Dará principio por ocupar todos los bienes pertenecientes á las Misiones de ambas Californias' (occupy ALL mission property of both Californias; the military commander to furnish force); one-year term; colonists' town-lots (≤ 500 varas, solares within the traced street-lines); each colonist family gets in full ownership *caballerías* of land (1 if irrigated / 16 if grazing), 4 cows, 2 ox-teams or 2 bulls, 2 tame horses, 4 colts, 4 fillies, small stock + 12 fitted plows; no family sold > 200 head of one class (art. 12); half the surplus mission goods reserved by the general govt for worship, missionary *congrua*, primary-schoolteachers' pay & free farm tools for colonists (art. 13); Híjar to render annual accounts of mission-property products & the colony's state (arts. 14–15). The contested mission-occupation mandate Figueroa refused to execute — the legal heart of the Híjar–Padrés affair. ⚠ corrects the gap-sample's page estimate ('tomo pp. 370–371' → actual tomo pp. 270–273 / Sav. pp. 383–6)

summary: Figueroa's *informe reservado* on the Híjar–Padrés affair — the constitutional heart of it: because the 25 July 1834 supreme order separated Híjar from the political command, and his power to manage mission property was given him only *as* Gefe Político, 'habiendo cesado en este encargo, ninguna otra investidura le autorizaba'; the Diputación would be 'culpable' if it obeyed his pretensions, and does not consider the law authorizing the Supreme Govt to dispose of mission goods applicable. date_text: 1792, May 10, San Diego *(text dates to Neve's 1782 handover)*
author: Cmdt.-Gen. Pedro de Nava
summary: transmits a copy of Felipe de Neve's *Instrucción* to his successor Pedro Fages. *(✎ bounds & orig pp CORRECTED vs scans, 2026-07-02 verify pass: the Instrucción ENDS at n103 top, signed 'Parage del Saucito, á la Salida del Cajón de Santa Catarina 7 de Setᵉ de 1782 = Felipe de Neve,' Savage ref 'pp 440–63' — the old 'orig. pp. 72–105' was savage-page arithmetic, and the old '~n105' bound concealed 6 uncataloged docs, now Docs 70b–70e & 71b–71c below)* — Nava forwards the full text of ex-Gov. Felipe de Neve's handover *Instrucción* to Gov. Pedro Fages (Neve governed 1777–82), because the original was missing from the Cal. government archive (per the gov.'s oficio No. 88 of 21 Jan 1792). A long, article-numbered governance document (arts. 1–18+) spanning ~34 Savage pages. ⭐⭐ Major source for early-1780s administration of *both* Californias. Sampled content: (core policy) 'El principal objeto del acierto de Gobierno debe consistir en conservar en una perfecta paz y tranquilidad la Península, manteniendo la amistad y buen trato de todas las Naciones gentiles sin permitir se les persiga en modo alguno' — conciliation via small gifts ('uno á dos hilos de abalorios'). (Colorado/Yuma frontier, n76) the Quechan attacks — killing of Cabo Antonio Briones, fires set before Alférez José Velásquez's 50-mule pack-train; Neve's planned 40-man *entrada* 'para sorprenderlos en sus rancherías… sin hacerles guerra' was undone by 'la novedad ocurrida en el Colorado' (the 1781 Yuma Revolt). (graduated Indian discipline, n79–81) for stock-killing near Monterey/SF/San José/San Diego: 8–10 days *cepo* + 20–25 lashes for gentiles, *then* admonish & gift an *almud* of maize; names Fr. Junípero Serra (asked to admonish San Carlos neophytes who killed ~10 head of the Monterey *caballada*) and Fr. Peña at Santa Clara; rule that no religious accompany sorties to gentile rancherías. (presidio economy, n88) *matanza*/tallow/*tasajo* provisioning to wean the presidios off San Blas *manteca*. (Baja fiscal, n94–101) Loreto *alcabala*; the Real de Santa Ana silver *hacienda* sold to Capt. Antonio de Osio ($1,000); José de Gálvez's *bando* barring commerce with the Manila *nao*; mission-inventory accounting. (art. 17) a proposed Peninsula–Philippines commerce plan; (art. 18) relations with the Padre Presidente. → [[bay-area-borderlands project]], [[indian-raiding-article]], governance. ⚠️ Long doc — only sampled; a future pass could transcribe arts. fully.
cite: State Papers, Sacramento, MS, tom. I, p. 440–463, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 54, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 73–104 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n72–n103)

summary: Revilla Gigedo → Gov. of Cal. — 'Objeto de venida de hombres científicos.' *(NEW, 2026-07-02 verify pass)* — Acknowledges oficio of 3 Jan announcing the *Princesa*'s arrival at Loreto 'trayendo á su bordo 'al Naturalista Don José Longinos Martínez, y al Botánico Don Jaime Sencebo [Senseve], comisionados por S.M. con el objeto de colectar pª el Gabinete de Historia Natural las varias producciones de esa Provincia.'' ⭐ The viceregal statement of the Royal Scientific Expedition's purpose — pairs with Doc 70b (Nava's parallel ack.) and the Vancouver/Menzies science thread.

author: Juan Pablo Grijalva, Alférez, San Diego company

Borica's marginal endorsement (Monterey, May 1796): 'Me consta cuanto expresa el interesado… le considero acreedor' — grant retirement at half-pay of alférez + grade of teniente, for his 'celo, exactitud y valor.' → [[indian-raiding-article]], prosopography (Grijalva = Anza-expedition veteran).

summary: interim Gov. date_text: 1792-11-14, San Francisco *(arrival 'ayer al meterse el sol')*
author: Doc 77e
summary: [UNSIGNED: ¿Sgt. Pedro Amador ó Tte. Sal?] → Arrillaga — 'Llegada de Vancouver.' *(gap-recovery 2026-07-05 — was highlights-only)* — 'Ayer al meterse el sol entró en este puerto la fragᵃ de S.M.B. nombrada la 'Descubierta' (sic) del mando del Capᵗᵃⁿ de navío Dⁿ Jorge Vancouver, quien fondeó como á una legua más abajo del Presidio frente del parage que llamamos la Yerba buena'; Vancouver's packet forwarded same date to Bodega y Quadra ('le espera en San Francisco, ó con su aviso pasar á Monterey'); provisions = fresh meat/verdura/leña + flour, menestras, ship timbers; 'le he ofertado mi persona, casa, y cuanto en ella hubiere'; the soldado Alejo Miranda put aboard as práctico (name crop-verified). Ends: 'Sólo siento el hallarme tan falto de fuerzas con solo un cañón, y éste reventado' (the boundary-letter formula). Unsigned — Savage: 'se cree sea del Sargᵗᵒ Pedro Amador, por [quedar] encargado del Presidio'; pencil: 'más probable es que… Sal.' ⚠ letter's 'ayer' = 13 Nov vs Vancouver's journal 14 Nov — don't harmonize. → [[bodega-primary-sources]] #105, [[sal-papers]]
cite: State Papers, Sacramento, MS, tom. I, p. 618–21, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 54, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 116–118 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n115–n117)

summary: Sal → Arrillaga — 'Heridas en San José. Partida de Sal pᵃ dho punto.' *(gap-recovery 2026-07-05)* — By order of Tte. José Argüello, Sal goes to San José for a sumaria on the wounding of the vecino Claudio Alires [Alvires], 'dejando encargado del presidio al Sargᵗᵒ Pedro Amador' — the context for Doc 77e's attribution question (Amador in charge 1–~14 Nov).

author: Doc 77g
summary: Sal → Arrillaga — 'conclusión de los trabajos del presidio — Fuertes aguaceros. Mal estado de algᵒˢ edificios.' *(gap-recovery 2026-07-05)* — Works concluded: a 'lienzo de muralla de 26 varas para cerrar el triángulo' (comandante's house → almacén) + church/warehouse works + 9 troop houses renewed ('quedando de nuevos todos estos jacales'); rains 'cual no se han experimentado'; the families 'están como en el raso, de que estoy harto de verlo en este Presidio'; the 2nd officer's house 'se está viniendo á tierra' — build new? Written 4 days after Vancouver sailed — the Spanish twin of his SF-poverty description. → [[presidio-decay-project]]

Formal witness declarations (soldiers Acevedo, 'Gloria,' Juan Álvarez et al. — going to the rancherías, an *india* hurt) closing at San Juan Capistrano (21 Jun 1777, Guillermo Carrillo; cert. copy Ortega, San Diego Jul 1777) & the San Gabriel escort (1 Oct 1777). ⭐ Embeds a punitive skirmish at the ranchería *Alacua Chomi* (20 Jun 1777): a cabo + 5 soldiers attacked; gentiles loosed arrows (wounding Mathías López's & Acevedo's horses); soldiers fired, 3–4 Indians killed, 2 captured (one given 25 lashes); the gentiles had vowed to behead the 'cabo guapo' & threatened mission Christians — over soldiers stripping them of deer-skins & forcing their women. summary: The official account of the 1831 OVERTHROW OF VICTORIA (briefing the incoming governor; a long compiled narrative quoting Victoria's own letters — overlaps Doc 82). Narrates: the disputed Jan-1831 handover (Echeandía absent at SD; Victoria reaches Monterey 29 Jan «en estado de revolución»); Padrés's mission-plan = the 1813 Spanish-Cortes decree of 13 Sept (33 arts.) turning Indian/mission property over to the ordinaries; the plotters regroup at San Francisco w/ Alférez M. G. Vallejo & Sgt José Sánchez; boosted by May–Jun-1831 rumors of Guerrero's return to the Presidency; Mariano Duarte alcalde de San José among promoters; revolt erupts 29 Nov 1831 at the SD presidio; Victoria gravely wounded near Los Ángeles [Cahuenga]; expelled, writes from San Blas (6 Feb 1832) that the Diputación reunited at LA and named PÍO PICO Jefe político; ⭐⭐⭐⭐ names the faction — «dos hermanos de Carrillo, Bandini el comisario, Pío Pico, Santiago Argüello, un Americano del Norte [Stearns], José M. Padrés, y sobre todos Echeandía» (the ones «que fomentaron á los oficiales»). Then Echeandía's counter-account (via the Gov. of Sonora's 6 Feb letter): his 5 charges against Victoria — (1) refusing to convene the Diputación in the lawful archive, (2) protecting the deposed LA alcalde Vicente Sánchez, (3) ⭐ the decapitation of the Indian «Atanasio», (4) ⭐⭐⭐⭐ the banishment of José Antonio Carrillo & the exile of Abel STEARNS (the causation link for Stearns's role), (5) arbitrary «ejecuciones de justicia»; the 29 Nov SD pronunciamiento (3 demands: deny obedience to Victoria / reunite the Diputación / name provisional command), Portilla's march to LA, the 5 Dec Cahuenga action (Victoria «se retiró á San Gabriel» wounded, agrees to embark), the Diputación convoked 1 Jan 1832 (citing the 6 May 1822 subdivision decree); + the Diputación vocals Vallejo/Pico/Osio's formal complaint of 18 Sept 1831 against Victoria — *(runs on past n80)*

summary: The Goleta *LIDIA* foreign-ship causa (1826, 'Pieza 6ª') — READ IN FULL: contraband/foreign-trade enforcement proceedings over the RAC-connected schooner Lidia, arrested in the Santa Bárbara Channel at the Ensenada/Cala del Refugio (Rancho de los Ortega) pleading necessity of provisions. Three sworn declarations, translated from English by interpreter Romero: (1) an RAC sailor off the *Lidia* at Sitka; (2) ⭐ Guillermo (William) Mort, Protestant mariner of Glasgow, ~27; (3) ⭐⭐ the captain/first-pilot Enrique [Ezxelaar?], Lutheran, of Amsterdam, ~30. Testimony: the *Lidia* sailed Macao/Canton → Sitka, delivering the cargo (Chinese silks & papel de China, aguardiente de Batavia, 330 sacks salt, razors, tea, and mounted cannons) to the Russian Governor at Sitka; then coasted south (bound for the 'Islas Marcos' & back to Canton), put in at Refugio short of provisions, traded (a barrel of salmon) and was seized 'preso por el Rey.' Judge presses the prohibition on foreign trade; captain pleads absolute necessity. Also names Don Carlos Carrillo, the *Albatros*. → [[project_bodega_open_door]] 'Open Door'/foreign-trade + smuggling enforcement + [[russian-california]] (Sitka/RAC arms supply). Leaf refs internal 291–98, 299–300.

Complaint: Hyde (1º Alcalde) & Leavenworth (2º Alcalde) dishonor their high & responsible offices; the town 'has fallen into a disgraceful state of confusion & become the frequent theater of the most revolting scenes — riots, bloody street fights'; law & authority openly defied; the chief magistrate publicly insulting; the Alcalde is the associate of the gambler class & passes his nights in their company; petition to appoint Dr. John Townsend (first) & John C. Buchanan (2º Alcalde). A separate same-date petition recommends Townsend for first Alcalde. Same date W.A. Leidesdorff in a private letter to Gov. Mason: since the Gov. was last in SF, testimony has accumulated agt 1º Alcalde Geo. Hyde changing his opinion, prompting immediate removal — 'he alone has been the means of creating a state of affairs here which renders every gentleman liable to be insulted at the corners of the streets, and if resistance is made, he is either shot or stabbed, and the culprit is suffered to go at large'; Hyde suspected of being author of clerical scurrilous articles in the 'Californian' agt the council; the writer, since becoming a member of council, has been trying to have a law passed to put down gambling (of which McDougal & Lippincott are aware), 'they being gamblers by profession,' for which those persons as well as Alcalde Hyde are his personal enemies

The wild Indians are those who live in the mountains; those as far as the base of the mountains are only taken in this census; the whole side of the Californian mountain is thickly settled with wild Indians who are generally at war with the surrounding small tribes at the base, & do not visit the valley — their number I am not able to give; the Indns contained in this estimate are divided into abt 70 small tribes speaking some 20 different languages.' No schools in the district, the whites few, thinly scattered, 400 miles distant; a school house to be built next year in a town now being laid out 3 miles below the fort; a flouring mill by water power in operation, another & the saw mill will begin work in a few months; horse-power mills & the tannery have been in operation several years; dwelling houses principally of adobe, occupied by farmers

Kelly of Sonoma, a man of good standing & respectability; cause: an alleged insult & attempt at violence by the Indian to Kelly's wife; prior to the killing the Indian had been tried, before the magistrate & sentenced to receive 100 lashes; after the infliction of the punishment & discharge of the Indian, Kelly in company with several other persons went in quest of him, & upon finding him, Kelly deliberately drew a pistol & shot him thro' the head inflicting a mortal wound. 'Murders & outrages agt Indians frequent & committed with impunity — measures must & things must be adopted to stop that lawlessness, or else this community will be greatly endangered by retaliation on the part of the Indians.' [+ a long private-letter essay, orig. in Spanish, translated on margin by Wm. E.P. Hartnell:] 'I have sought at all times the means of regulating the management of Indns as well for their private benefit, as to amalgamate them as far as possible with the whites… This race of people appear to be a peculiar race, and in their youth capable of the best civilization, when they keep this age, then is no medical way of inducing them to leave their miserable manner of living like brutes… have so far many years the protection of the singular, unhappy & degraded race, which if it requires indeed all the protection of gout to civilize it & prevent from atrocious deviations, it is at the same time necessary that it should feel the weight of an iron hand, for otherwise the white race will perish… Vagabondism, scandalous drunkenness, robberies, wounds & murders are committed by the Indns in this jurisdiction with great frequency… they understand liberty has broken the reins of subordination; and if this is civilized society, is an evil of great consequence.' Recommends: imposing fines & confinement on all thefts & violations of the peace/spirituous liquors & theft; that persons in whose employ the Indians are be made responsible for them, except in criminal cases; that they deliver up to competent authority all seditious Indians; that a place be appointed in each pueblo for gathering together such Indians as have no fixed residence, so that their conduct may be closely watched, appoint of alcaldes from among themselves who shall make daily report of occurrences to the nearest authority; & jefe títulos to have officiers & strong prison built for shutting up those who do wrong, making them labor at pub. works; & that a military cavalry force be established to be destined solely for the persecution & vigilance of the Indians, at present consisting of not less than 15 men

author: John Forster (Alcalde)

Fisher would make a very good Alcalde but couldn't be prevailed on to accept; the best one after him is Charles White; election of a new town council impossible; asks a promiscuous body of 25 men of U.S. troops be stationed there to guard the prison-officers & aid the alcaldes arresting refractory convicts

author: Gov. Mason

author: Gov. [George] Abernethy (Gov. of Oregon)
summary: On supplies of ammunition & condition of Oregon: rec'd the liberal supplies of arms & ammunition sent by Mason; 'should the period of U.S. be extended over us, or troops come out for our protection, will immediately, on their arrival turn all over to the proper officers'; difficulties with Indians ceased, the murderers fled, other tribes profess friendship for U.S.; white men have 'all gone to the mining region, not less than 3000 leave the valley for Cal., most will return, having left their families looking'; immigrants this year have not been molested on their journey by the Indians (the gold rush emptying Oregon); 'the rec't of the ordnance & ordnance stores sent by you gives a feeling of satisfaction to every American in the territory — it looks as if they were not deserted by their country… should the Indians trouble again, we feel that we are well supplied with arms and ammunition'

summary: By Gov. Mason's appt

author: Commodore James Biddle

Nash (late Alcalde at Sonoma) & John Ricord (late Attorney Genl at Sandwich Islds): says Nash is on board his ship, has requested Commodore to intercede with Gov. on his behalf, is sensible of his error & if forgiven will behave peaceably — will be sent to Mont. on a U.S. Ship, will have a good effect. Says John Ricord is a notorious scoundrel who ran away several years ago from U.S. with a large sum of money belonging to another; been cause of much vexation & trouble to Americans in Sandwich Islands; 'a villain that should not be trusted'; intends to come & settle in Cal., will try to insinuate himself in the Gov's favor; 'for Heaven's sake, for your own sake, for the sake of the peace & quietness of the country, give him no employment or countenance whatever'

cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 144 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n144)

author: Capt. [Wm.] Brackett
summary: On armed opposition in Sonoma & Northern Cal.: courts as at present constituted bring justice into disrepute; the old man now acting as Alcalde (Nash) ignorant, conceited & dogmatical, governed by whims, without regard to law; a runaway sailor by the name of Green has obtained a strong influence over him; the present unlimited & illegal powers assumed then the country by the diff. Alcaldes will give rise to much confusion & litigation; will continue acting on events & all matters connected with Gen. Kearny's administration in Cal.
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 145 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n145)

author: Col. R.B. Mason
summary: On missions of San José & Santa Clara — horse-thieves & necessity for a prison on the San Joaquín river: visited the missions, examined into complaints of Padres & Cal.; found emigrants in possession who have injured the buildings very seriously, removing doors/windows/tile & the vineyards also damaged; at San José the emigrants did not even ask for the key to enter the buildings — they broke open the doors, & took entire possession, not even leaving the room occupied by the priest when he visits; much damage; there is no need of stationing troops at pueblo de San José, they could not prevent the Indians stealing the people's horses & their action — Indians come in small parties of two or three from different directions, must at some preconcerted place & commence their operations, carrying off from time to time 200 or 300 head, & are in constant communication with those at the ranchos; recommends a company be stationed on West bank of the San Joaquín river; there are three passes over the mountains by either one of which the Indians must pass with their stolen horses before reaching the San Joaquín; 'it might be good policy to add to that company 30 native citizens of Cal., mounted volunteers, to serve 12 months, with same pay & rations, & allowance for horses & clothing, as allowed by law'
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 146 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n146–147)

author: C.E. Bartlett
summary: Opinion on public affairs, men & measures: something must be done quickly to avert the horrors that yet await this unhappy land; all is turmoil & confusion; only by the establishment of a good govt & a proper code of laws will we give the country peace & quiet; there is good reason to suspect intolerable & revolutionary movements on foot which must be nipped in the bud; Gov. must not expect to obtain correct information [from natives]...
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 147 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n147–148)

author: C.E. Bartlett
summary: (cont. of doc 251) Candid character-sketch of officeholder candidates & broad denunciation of the naval/Frémont regime: warns of 'disaffected men, dishonest & scheming, at whose head are Stockton & others, whose lawless acts have… damaged their reputations'; 'the mad, lawless & tyrannical schemes and acts of Frémont, Stockton, & other officers of the Navy on shore, have produced a lukewarmness in the hearts of many true Amns'; the Alcaldes throughout Cal. have been since the raising of the flag 'but a mockery to law & justice, assuming & exercising prerogatives & powers far beyond any clothed them by the Mexn or U.S. laws… a total disregard of all law, justice, reason and right'; on judges: Bryant, Alcalde of SF, 'a man of education, honest & pure, but for all that unfit for judge or legislator… his reasoning faculties are bad'; Hastings 'too little talent… strongly suspected of being leagued with the Mormons'; Jones 'has talent enough, but is a Mormon, and a villain of the deepest dye'; Russell 'a mere bag of puffed-up, bloated wind'; recommends looking among the recent overland emigrants for strong-minded upright men
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 148 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n148–150)

author: Col. Stevenson
summary: Proceedings about a cannon stolen at Sta Bárbara; inhabitants made to pay for it; the July-4-1848 celebration & the Sta Bárbara alcaldes' resignations: pursuant to order went to Sta Bárbara 19 June, arrived 21st; interviewed chief inhabitants, suggested their offering a reward of $100 to have the gun (cannon) or that reward offered to any one who would inform Padre González, under decree of the Confessional — the Padre secured he would not be required to reveal informant's name. 26 June caused a list of all inhabitants of 20 years & up to be published, posted at the usual places; up to 1 July collected but $100; on 2 July made an assessment on real & personal property according to best information, sent each a note stating amt of his assessment, required prompt payt by 7 p.m. July 4 — result was payt of abt $250; made levies on the property of two: one, a Mr. Uren, Irish but naturalized citizen of Mex., the other Mr. Scott [Wilson], firm of Scott & Wilson, who refused to pay his share because he was not a citizen of Mex. — both insolent & rude in refusals; several persons promised payt as loan as they could raise the money; several had to sell their cattle & horses at sacrifice; total collected $365, & Capt. Lippitt charged with collection of the balance. Detail: when he reached Sta Bárbara the inhabitants were determined not to pay the fine, but on being informed he assessed the principal inhabitants at a 'course reasonable, however painful… enforce the order, seizing property enough to cover the full amt, they could in no way escape the payt'; result satisfactory & people behaved better than any portion of Amns at home under similar circumstances. The two Alcaldes Pedro C. Carrillo & Ardison protest agt the payt, 'in consequence of holding Commissions under the Gov.'; they resigned their commissions but he did not accept the resignations, advising them not to attempt to protect the Gov's dignity, which they seemed to consider vulnerable, for the Gov. could take good care of his own dignity; Mr. Scott's protest was answered by telling him it would be referred to the Gov. Only two persons exempt from the fine (both Americans, who furnished evidence of services rendered to U.S.). The stolen cannon (of Brig Elizabeth): the gun together with 2 carronades sent to the beach by Capt. Lippitt for being carried by the Brig's master, but the master neglected to take them, they lay on the beach 5 or 6 days; finally offered to sell the gun to Capt. of Brig Louisa — bargain complete except the gun had to be delivered at Monterey, but somehow the gun had disappeared the same night; Capt. of the Elizabeth had failed to pay his men, they were dissatisfied & made threats to destroy his property; it is believed they concealed the gun; the gun was marks that it had been dragged sideways on the beach to the edge of the water where it disappeared; suspicion it was done with by the sailors; the $100 reward would have brought out the matter if any Californian had a hand in it. During his visits a great desire was expressed to hear a band of music — none had been heard except Commodore Stockton's when the town was taken — then they only play'd 'Yankee Doodle' & 'Star Spangled Banner'; determined to gratify them dispatched a wagon to bring the leader & his band & music (esp. old Sp. music); band arrived evening of 3 July under an officer commanding, playing French/Sp./Mexn pieces; next morning all came to thank him, & he allowed the fandango/ball given by the officers; that day the principal inhabitants also present at the celebration by himself, his officers, men & attendants of the 4th of July anniversary; manifested much interest & gratification; he had to speak of Amn victories in Mexico 'but did it without wounding their feelings, & expatiated upon the kindness & hospitality of the Californians & the friendly relations existing between them & the Americans since a legitimate govt & Commander was in the country'; on 6 July when he was leaving the town all the principal natives came to take leave of him; concludes hoping the Gov. will think the Californians were innocent of the disappearance of the gun
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 151 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n151–155)

author: Col. Stevenson

author: J.L.W. Hastings
summary: Accepts the judgeship for the Northern Dist. tendered him by the Gov., 'altho' agt his interests, in his desire to see some system of laws & govt established'; disorderly state of the region — murders & robbery of frequent occurrence; 'selling liquor to Indians is fully practised by many whenever it suits their purposes of gain'
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 157 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n157)

author: John Townsend, C.V. Gillespie, S. Brannan & 26 other prominent business men
summary: Petition Gov. to order an election for two members of the Common Council to fill vacancies occasioned by resignation of Glover & death of Leidesdorff; Council now reduced to 4, held no meeting for want of quorum; it would be well members could have authority to preside as Justices of the Peace; also necessary to appoint a harbor master; recommend appt of 3 Port-Wardens to choose Harbor masters & examine such persons as desire to serve as pilots — Collector of Port to be ex-officio member of the Board of Port Wardens

author: Col. Stevenson

cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 159 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n159)

author: Col. Stevenson
summary: Civil-Govt troubles with the Alcaldes & satisfactory results (the full LA Alcalde-Foster reinstatement narrative, cf. docs 104b/228): acknowledges receipt of Gov's communication of Dec 10 enclosing commission of Stephen C. Foster as Alcalde of the dist., together with a letter to the Alcalde directing him to turn over books & papers & other property to his successor Mr. Foster; the Foster commission enclosed in one from Mr. Stearns, expressing fully the reasons the Alcalde [Palomares] declined the Sept appt of Mr. Foster; on 1 Sept the old town Ayuntamiento assembled, ready to receive communication; Stevenson immediately presented himself with Mr. Foster, introduced him as the Alcalde appointed by the Gov. for the year 1848; stated Foster should be at once put to exercise his office, & subsequently (if this don't necessary) they only administer to him the oath of office in usual form of the country; requiring the [old] Alcalde to deliver over the archives; one of the Ayuntamiento inquiring if this election of alcaldes was to be disregarded, or whether their alcaldes would be permitted to act, & Mr. Foster assume the duties of Juez de 1ª Instancia which would give him control of all their actions without violation of the ancient privileges of the town; Stevenson replied he had no power to change it, & if they, individually or collectively, felt aggrieved, would with great pleasure take charge of memorial/protest they chose to prepare, but his duty required he should see Gov's order executed; then required to swear in Foster & required all present to obey; Ml. Requena[?], Alcalde of 1847, permitted to turn over the pub. records & property to the elected successor de Palomares, provided he close to be sworn into office; a committee from the Ayuntamiento waited on Stevenson with the respectful reports of the Corporation that seconded permit their Alcaldes to be sworn into office & enter on their duties, agreeing that Foster as Juez de 1ª Instancia should supervise; the pub. interest would be better served by the proposed arrangement & Foster relieved of the trifling business incumbent on an Alcalde's office & better able to devote his time to more important public matters; Stevenson consented, provided the Ayuntamiento make the request in writing; on Monday at 10 o'clock the committee returned, all officers sworn in & a committee appointed to make the written communication; regarded as a formal resignation of the entire Ayuntamiento, leaving Foster Alcalde without any person to aid him in the civil govt of the town, distinctly stated the Ayuntamiento would not accept any office under him; the first business in order was to feed the prisoners & pay a guard for the prison; result satisfactory
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 159 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n159–163)

author: José Salazar (Alcalde this whole year), Ignº Coronel (Secretary)
summary: Note of office; P.S. to doc 257 noting one of the 6 enclosed docs: Stevenson to Alcalde Salazar that 'owing to neglect on the part of the authorities, the town had become the resort of prostitutes & vagrants of the most depraved character, the pub. interests neglected, and the collection of debts or punishment of criminals impossible'
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 167 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n167)

author: Wm. G. Dana (Alcalde)
summary: Indian depredations — bad state of society at San Luis Obispo: society reduced to the most trying state; the pueblo place for a long time past a complete sink of drunkenness & debauchery; Alcalde endeavored unsuccessfully by want of force to restore order; there were respectable Amns on their farms at some distance from the mission, 'and it is really impossible that they could unite (in case of an outbreak) in season to be of any service; a military force absolutely necessary in the place; the wild Indians committing raids carrying off drove of horses; Californians & foreigners formed a party & went after them — in a week returned; found the Indians too strong; if some prompt measures are not adopted, the farmers will have to abandon their ranchos; horrid murders are reported at San Luis by the Alcalde — unnecessary massacre'
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 168 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n168)

author: Wm. Richardson[?] (Alcalde eastern part SF Bay)
summary: Indian depredations: took a stroll by the Contra Costa of SF, having heard great complaints agt the Indians; conversed with the Chief Magistrate of the dist., Don Joaquín Estudillo, found him anxious to do all in his power to check them; advised the Gov. on the best means of procuring Native-Cal. volunteers to accompany the troops; the wild Indians committing raids carrying off horses; sent after them, were seen, but succeeded in escaping — want of horses prevents them being pursued

summary: THE ARMIJO/EGGER/SMITH TRIAL (Spanish version, cf. ⭐⭐⭐ doc 185): per instructions to try the criminal cause against Armijo, Egger y Smith for the Sacramento Indian killings, presented himself at Sutter's on the 30th; on the 31st a tribunal was set & copy of the accusation given the accused, save Armijo (absent, gravely ill, cannot be moved); Samuel Smith had come as an agent of all the upper-Sacramento people, saying some Indians had found several corpses supposed killed by Armijo & his party; Sutter deposed that S. author: Mariano Pacheco
summary: 'Relación de su viaje en busca de oro': a first-person GOLD-PROSPECTING EXPEDITION NARRATIVE — the trip made by the tulareños was fatal; on reaching the rancherías of the Sonoltas some companions announced a catastrophe the Sierra Indians would cause, at the point they meant to seek gold; some went to inspect the Sierra called del Río de Reyes [Kings River], but there was no gold; at the 3-day reunion at the rancherías de los Guileches, they had earlier found a large number of Yaqui[?] Indians who had stalked them; all resolved to turn back; determined to seek the San Joaquín where at Bautista's there was gold-working; Guillermo with 7 men went ahead to look for people, & 3 leagues on with his companions, thinking to find the workers, met disaster — the Sierra Indians, ~300 at the ranchería del Chabailes, fired: Guillermo Gama, Faustino García, Bartolo Olivera, Francisco Archuleta, [Juan] Manuel of Nuevo México, Francisco Presidio[?], Sonora, y José Mª Salazar killed; only Lorenzo Espinosa of Nuevo México survived, hidden 4 days in a cave; Frémont with 30 men refused to go recover the corpses as futile; the emigrants lose hope of gold & flee the region for the danger — ⭐⭐⭐ a named-casualty account of a fatal 1849 Sierra gold-hunt & Indian ambush, Frémont implicated in the abandonment

summary: THE SAN JUAN BAUTISTA ELECTION-FRAUD + VAIL/WAIT LAND-DESPOLIATION AFFAIR: (a) the Comisión de Elecciones' queja against the Juzgado of San Juan Bautista — the Juez José María Sánchez refused to accept the Governor's order to verify the elections, having made the Junta de vecinos convened for the purpose fail; the querella adds (Lehiya[?]) that Sánchez was found 'muy borracho junto con otros individuos también borrachos, en un lugar por donde pasaban Lehiya y sus compañeros'; the Comisión asks the sentencias of not having verified the elections be sent to the Governor; (b) ⭐⭐ Antonio Mª Pico, Prefecto (30 Nov 1849): 'Despojos de terrenos cometidos por el Medir[?] Wait/Vail' — several vecinos have suffered attacks & despojos in their properties (casas y terrenos) because the ex-Juez Wait formed a bogus 'Junta del Pueblo' with other American citizens & divided the pueblo lots into blocks (manzanas) of more than one league square, whose lands he took, dispossessing the vecinos & the mission of its most valuable lands; at the first junta only 4 or 5 vecinos of the country (Californians) & the rest Americans attended, & the act was written in English, so no one gave Wait authorization to redistribute lands; the Ayuntamiento's efforts to remedy met opposition; Pico names Francisco Vaca[?] as comisionado of the Prefectura to report fully — ⭐⭐ a documented American land-grab dispossessing Californios & the mission at San Juan Bautista, prosecuted by the Californio prefect
cite: Miscellaneous / Unbound Documents, MS, Archives of California, BANC MSS C-A 63, Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley; Savage transcript p. 361 (original destroyed 1906; digitized scan n363–366)
